item.title: Cerebras Readies CS-5 Systems For 2027 Launch As It Bags Another Hyperscaler
item.description:
Upstart waferscale AI compute maker Cerebras Systems has been very upfront for all of 2026 that this was a year to build out its cloud and to ramp up its manufacturing capability so it can start meeting the demands of the contracts it has inked with OpenAI and now Amazon Web Services, Oracle Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Thus far, most of its revenue backlog and all of its incremental revenue is coming from that OpenAI deal, which is finally ramping.

Next year is going to be a banner year for many AI system providers, and there is a non-zero chance that this could be the peak spending year for the GenAI boom. We shall see, and even AI systems do a terrible job at predicting the future. All anyone knows is what their customers tell them, and all those organizations know is what their customers tell them, and so on down and up the chain of being. Bullshit sometimes begets even bigger bullshit, but sometimes it isn’t bullshit and people really do buy a ton of systems. Which has happened for the past four years now despite the fears that the gravy train might run out of coal.

Here is the thing, though: This GenAI thing is real. It is just a matter of time, driven by ever-decreasing cost of token chewing and spitting, before it becomes pervasive in the world’s applications, or around the world’s applications. Some go too far and think as the world’s applications, and that is because they do not understand the nature of risk avoidance by the millions of corporations around the world. There is mainframe code older than me at the center of our banking and insurance systems, and wave after wave of technological evolution since I entered the IT sector four decades ago has augmented that code but a very large portion of it is still there, like a granite mountain.

In the third quarter, Cerebras didn’t sell as much of its CS-3 and CS-4 hardware as it has done in prior quarters, and that stands to reason because the company was building out its cloud services business in support of the $10 billion inference deal that the company inked with AI model builder OpenAI back in January 2026.

Since then, that deal, for 750 megawatts of gear that OpenAI can rent for fast inference, has been expressed as being worth $20 billion and sometimes $30 billion between 2026 and 2032, inclusive. That larger revenue stream is apparently possible if OpenAI has Cerebras build an additional 1.25 gigawatts of capacity by the end of 2030 and the contract for services runs out to 2032. Provided OpenAI goes public and has the cash, there is no reason to believe that it will not stretch this deal to the max. This option by definition has to be cheaper than buying Nvidia GPUs for inference prefill and Nvidia Grok LPUs for decode. Particularly with Cerebras using AMD GPUs for prefill, as it is doing in its cloud.

In the third quarter, hardware sales at Cerebras were down 28.8 percent to $68.9 million, and because the Cerebras factory is still ramping to a new production level gross margins were pretty bad at only 11 percent of revenues instead of the long-term goal of 60 percent. Andrew Feldman, co-founder and chief executive officer at the company, told Wall Street analysts in a conference call that margins in Q3 2026 were also adversely affected by the aggressive pricing that an early customer – presumably cloud provider G42 – negotiated years ago for machines being installed now.

The has been some jawboning out there on the intertubes that Cerebras has a yield problem, and Feldman brought the boot down on that idea. And it stands to reason. The WSE-3 used in the CS-3 systems and the WSE-3 Turbo used in the CS-4 systems are based on very mature 5 nanometer processes from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co – nothing crazy like the 2 nanometer processes that AMD is spearheading with its “Venice” Epyc 9006 server CPUs, just launched this week. The WSE-3 Turbo is a stop-gap, double-clocked waferscale processor that Cerebras put into the market in August in the CS-4 systems and there is a WSE-5 (you can’t have a WSE-4 because there isn’t going to be one) in the works for next summer for the CS-5 machines. These CS-4 and CS-5 systems will compete with new GPUs from Nvidia and AMD and LPUs and other XPUs from Grok (essentially owned by Nvidia), SambaNova, Rebellions, and the homegrown gear from the hyperscalers, cloud builders, and AI model builders themselves.

“Our product road map continues to advance rapidly,” Feldman explained on the call. “Our CS-4 will soon be in full production, doubling both performance and throughput. Our next-generation processor, the Wafer Scale Engine 5, which will be deployed in our fifth-generation CS-5 system, is back from the fab ahead of schedule. The WSE-5 taped out on June 15. The chip is back, has been brought up, and is already running models and is undergoing in-chassis testing. Moving from tape-out to system test in less than five months is exceptional execution. The CS-5 will more than double the speed of CS-4. It will enter production in early summer of 2027. It is built on TSMC's 5 nanometer node, where competition for wafers is less intense and wafer costs are much lower.”

It is safe to say that that WSE-5 has been in development for a long time, and I strongly suspect that as technology has advanced, it has been tweaked to incorporate new things. I think there are all kinds of technological possibilities for this WSE-5 engine, including silicon photonics optical connections linking wafers and memory servers and SRAM stacking – two that I favor for the sake of Cerebras. At Hot Chips this past summer, Cerebras revealed that it would be using 3D stacked DRAM with its wafers.

I also think that given the need for fast inference, the wafers will be double-clocked from this point forward. Performance trumps power consumption and heat dissipation these days – dollars per millions of tokens is what matters more than dollars per millions of tokens per watt at this stage of GenAI commercialization. Electricity is cheaper than the systems, even if it is getting harder and harder to come by. Cerebras can always offer two different clock speeds at the same price and let customers decide.

We shall see next summer. . . .

Given the lumpiness of hardware sales at all supercomputer makers – and make no mistake, the CS family is comprised of supercomputers – it is best to look at the company’s financials on an annual, not quarterly basis. Here is how 2022 through 2025 and projections for GAPP revenue (mine), not the non-GAAP revenue (which is larger) that Cerebras talks about in its financial presentations for Q3 and Q4:

And for those of you who like the raw numbers, here are the quarterly and annual results in the typical TPM monster table:

My best guess is that on a GAAP basis, Cerebras will close 2026 with around $885 million in revenues, up 73.4 percent compared to 2025’s sales. Operating income and net income were whacked by a spike in research and development spending and stock-based compensation. Feldman said on the Wall Street call that the company expected to triple its sales in 2027, and it is reasonable to assume that as manufacturing ramps and Cerebras increases its margins on hardware with partners Flex and Sanmina that gross profits and operating income will be much improved in 2027.

Cerebras ended the third quarter with $7.36 billion in cash and equivalents in the bank and a revenue backlog of $26.1 billion, mostly from the OpenAI deal. The AWS, Oracle, and Microsoft deals are not yet in the backlog and are certainly not yet bringing in revenue. Cerebras has been pretty vague about what these deals are, but it is important to note that three of the biggest clouds in the world are going to be working CS iron into their inference workloads, presumably for decode operations. Whatever WSE-5 and the resulting CS-5 system is, this is what they almost certainly want, especially given that WSE-5 will have 2X the performance of the WSE-3 Turbo compute engine that is available now.

item.title: The Nvidia Machine Is Self-Sustaining – And Was Already Facing A Tougher Future
item.description:
Well, like most of you on Earth, I didn’t see that coming.

The third and most important of the co-founders of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has resigned as president and chief executive officer and Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer of the company, has been tapped as his interim replacement in the wake of the revelation of two affairs by Huang – one with an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed International (who may be a Chinese government operative) and another with an executive in the top ranks at Nvidia itself.

There is a lot of chatter that Megaspeed was channeling either Nvidia-based GPU systems or remote access to them (or both) to Chinese companies, including upstart model maker DeepSeek, and it is not clear if Huang knew this when a sister company of Megaspeed bought $4.8 billion in Nvidia GPU gear between June 2024 and February 2026. The Information is reporting that Megaspeed and its affiliates have acquired $7.5 billion in GPU systems since 2023. The US Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, according to the timeline put together by the New York Times , but those investigations apparently stalled as President Trump and Jensen Huang started getting chummy last year. The investigations were moved over to the US Department of Justice, and it is unclear what state they are in.

Suffice it to say, the new Congress being sworn in coming January 2027 will be all over this issue, and eventually facts will be gathered and punishments will be meted out as appropriate – and a presidential pardon for Jensen Huang should he be indicted for being complicit in the smuggling of systems made by Inspur into China or the renting of capacity on systems to Megaspeed customers like Alibaba.

It is not clear that the latter is yet illegal, but if you are putting export controls on physical machines, it only makes sense that you should have export controls on selling capacity from a cloud over the wires. In any event, Alibaba obviously builds its own AI models and would benefit from having access to Nvidia GPUs that are under export controls and are forbidden to be sold to organizations in China. It is also not clear where Megaspeed got its money to buy GOU systems and to build datacenters in Indonesia and China, but it is reasonable to infer that it stretches back into China.

Let the chips fall where they may.

For now, Harvey Jones, who was once chief executive officer at chip design software maker Synopsis and who is a managing partner with venture capitalist Square Wave Ventures, has been tapped as chairman of the board. This is the first time Nvidia has had a chairman. Jones has been on the board of Nvidia since November 1993, shortly after the company was founded in April 1993. The board is starting a CEO search to replace Huang and Kress, and there is every reason to believe that Kress will continue in her role as CFO in the wake of the new CEO coming in.

Aside from all of these issues, the biggest one is how the AI industry and Nvidia within it will work without Jensen Huang in the middle of it, being the ambassador for the AI future as well as its biggest beneficiary of the GenAI revolution that no company has capitalized on better than Nvidia. (That revolution has made Huang the 15 th richest person in the world, with $145 billion of Nvidia stock ahead of the affair revelations earlier this week.) Huang has to give up $108 million in share compensation by stepping down, and his 3.6 percent stake in Nvidia is also taking some lumps, but he will have plenty of capital to start something new if he so desires to do so. It seems likely that Huang will try to lay low for a while, and try to heal his relationships with his wife and children. The world will likely not let him lay low.

As for Nvidia, Huang is famous for running a tight ship and for having the company’s 60 top executive directly report to him so he knew exactly what everyone was doing and why. The good news for Nvidia is that this process is in place, and each of these five dozen executives are well acquainted with their jobs. Moreover, the Nvidia AI system roadmaps are set for the “Rubin” and “Feynman” generations of GPUs that will carry the company into 2030, and Nvidia’s production is sold out for 2027 already and it won’t be long before it is sold out for 2028 if history and increasing demand is any guide. If there was a time where Nvidia can largely run itself, it is now.

That said, Nvidia has never faced so many pressures from so many different forces at the same time.

The hyperscalers, cloud builders, and AI model builders are all working on their own custom CPUs and XPU AI accelerators to not only wean themselves off of very expensive Nvidia iron and to create hardware specifically to run their own AI models for around half of what it costs to do it with the Nvidia hardware and systems software stack.

Moreover, Nvidia is championing open source and open weight AI models – something only Nvidia can afford to do because it gets such a high premium for its AI compute and networking hardware. These open Nemotron models directly compete against the closed source and usually closed weight models of its largest GPU accelerator customers, which probably has them irked a bit.

But even more alarming for those who have enjoyed the meteoric rise of Nvidia during the GenAI boom, it is not clear that the rosy forecasts for AI spending out in 2029 and 2030 and beyond can be met because of supply chain constraints for many components as well as the difficulty of adding more electricity capacity to the grids of the world.

And in America at least, there is rising dissatisfaction for what is perceived of as preferential treatment that datacenter operators have enjoyed for the past decade and a half. It is not a coincidence that residential electric bills have gone up as datacenters have proliferated, and people are annoyed by the elitist attitudes of the tech titans who control AI. They are also rightly concerned with what GenAI will do to the economies, societies, and cultures of the world.

Finally, by Huang exiting the top job at Nvidia, the AI industry just got a lot less coherent and eloquent. And now we will find out just how important Huang would have been in a future that was already much less certain for Nvidia before he was compelled to leave the company.

item.title: CoreWeave Is Accelerating To Escape Velocity Thanks To GPU Shortages
item.description:
CoreWeave, arguably the king of the neoclouds that focus exclusively on AI processing as opposed to the full breadth of compute in the datacenter, has had its share of doubters and critics. And the consequent whipsawing around of its share price and people go bull or bear on it.

But thanks to the undersupply of GPUs in the world and the extreme desire to use them to train AI models and to run inference workloads against them, pricing for the vintage GPUs in the CoreWeave fleet are going up and up and up, and that means the company’s revenues are also rising and, not at all coincidentally but quite deliberately, so is CoreWeave’s operating profits. Which is all well and good. But the heavy debt load that CoreWeave has – roughly $48 billion by our math – is very expensive to service.

But here is the thing. That debt is being used to fund capital expenses that expand the CoreWeave datacenter footprint and its AI server fleet, and the quicker it builds out this fleet, the quicker it can start booking revenue against it. Companies are prepaying billions of dollars for capacity ahead of time, which is now being used to fund capex as well, and an even larger increase in demand for GPUs or a crimping of supply would only help CoreWeave make more money sooner.

In short, the economics of the GenAI boom are starting to play in CoreWeave’s favor, which company co-founder and chief executive officer Michael Intrator explained as part of his going over the company’s financial results for the third quarter of 2026.

“In July, we increased pricing across SKUs by approximately 25 percent, followed by another 10 percent increase later in the quarter,” Intrator explained. “Pricing has continued to move higher in Q4, more than offsetting cost increases. We are also allocating more capacity to short-term opportunities where the pricing justifies it, selling capacity at more than $40 million per megawatt annually, while pricing for new infrastructure on four- and five-year contracts is moving to $20 million to $25 million per megawatt. Long-term commitments provide the visibility that supports our build-out. Short-term contracts let us respond to a strong pricing environment and earn premium returns. We weigh that trade-off contract by contract, assessing the full economics of an investment, the revenue it can earn, the cost of operating it, and the cost of financing it. Strong demand gives us choices in how we best create durable value.”

To make his point, Intrator added that rental prices for Nvidia “Ampere” A100 GPUs in the CoreWeave fleet rose by 30 percent sequentially in the third quarter, and rental prices for “Hopper” H100 and H200 GPUs rose by 50 percent sequentially. That’s pretty damned good for the A100s, which are six and a half years old (they started shipping in May 2020), and the H100s, which are four years old (they started shipping in September 2022). The A100s have been written down completely is my guess and the H100s are probably going to be written down entirely next year. This means selling their capacity is very profitable even after taking out operating costs for the systems that use these vintage GPUs.

To further make his point, Intrator said that 130,000 GPUs would come off contract and be open for new deals at higher prices, and another 170,000 GPUs would be up for renewal in 2028. (My guess is that CoreWeave has around 1.25 million GPUs installed right now, based on its active power, just to give you a sense of how small a part of the fleet the renewals in 2027 and 2028 represent.) Intrator did a little math and said that the 2027 renewals would generate $4 billion in incremental annualized revenues at the current (and higher) prices and this would grow to an incremental $10 billion annualized revenues for the 2028 renewals.

“If datacenter construction across the sector were to slow, installed compute becomes scarcer and the knock-on effect is that GPU pricing may stay higher for longer,” Intrator explained. “In that scenario, being first matters. Our installed base comes off contract, fully paid, years ahead of most others in the market. We're well positioned across a range of market conditions. If the industry builds quickly, we grow with it. If supply is delayed, our installed paid-off fleet becomes more valuable. We do not build our plan on that scenario. The plan rests on contracted demand, success-based capex and the contracts we are already signing.”

All of this is why the chart below makes sense:

There is a direct correlation to the size of the CoreWeave GPU fleet, which I have estimated based on the active power each quarter, and the revenue backlog that CoreWeave is able to build. The correlation is very strong, as you can see. And it makes perfect sense.

But like a shark, the business has to keep moving to keep building that backlog, and at some point the debt load has to stop growing faster than revenues. That has to happen before the GenAI bubble bursts. I still believe that it will be very hard to find the power for the buildout that is expected in the IT sector in 2029 and 2030. We seem to be relatively safe in 2027 and into 2028, given so much of the capacity purchased is prepaid.

In the third quarter ended in September, CoreWeave booked $3.66 billion in sales, up 2.7X year on year and up 42.2 percent sequentially from the second quarter. Operating income was actually a positive $207 million, compared to an operating income of $52 million a year ago. But because of the debt service, the company’s net loss expanded by a factor of 6.4X to $709 million. Hence, losses are outpacing revenue growth. Not taking on more debt and using the proceeds from price increases to fund capex expansion – which is indeed the plan – will help get things back into whack. Or more precisely, into whack for the first time in CoreWeave’s history.

We shall see. But, the price increases and the demand to support them are encouraging signs.

If you like to drill down into the numbers yourself, here are the trends since Q1 2024:

CoreWeave exited the quarter with just under $5.6 billion in cash and equivalents and shelled out $14.5 billion for capital expenses. For the year so far, CoreWeave has spent $30.7 billion on datacenter gear and facilities. The company ended the quarter with a revenue backlog of $132.5 billion, up 2.4X year on year.

item.title: How The “Venice” Epycs Measure Up Against Prior AMD Server CPUs
item.description:
Over the past decade, each generation of Epyc processors from AMD is more complex and that complexity is leveraged not because the company’s top techies are baroque, but because it takes actual engineering distinctions to address the widening number and kind of workloads in the modern datacenter.

With the “Venice” generation of Epyc chips that launch today – the sixth generation and one that will once again put more water between itself and X86 CPU rival Intel – AMD is bringing to bear two different server sockets, two different I/O dies, and two different compute dies to create a product line that initially has 31 different CPUs initially, spanning from 8 cores to 256 cores, 130 watts to 600 watts, and from $700 to $14,904 when purchased in 1,000-unit trays from the company.

We have already discussed how AMD believes the Venice Epycs address today’s workload needs and also very generally how they compare to alternatives from X86 rival Intel and the Arm collective. This story walks through the Venice SKU stack and how the top bin and middle bin parts compare to the prior five generations of Epycs and the touchstone “Shanghai” quad-core Opteron processors were launched way back at the beginning of the Great Recession in November 2008.

The Salient Feeds And Speeds

Before we dive into the SKUs, we need to talk a little tech.

Rather than keep the Zen 6 and Zen 6c designs in distinct processor families within the Venice line, as AMD has done during the prior “Genoa” and “Turin” generations, the company has decided to blur the distinction between the Zen 6 and Zen 6 cores by keeping the cache hierarchies the same but in optimizing the schedulers inside the two cores in different ways – one optimized for higher core counts and lower clock speeds on the core compute dies (CCDs) and the other optimized for lower cores and higher clock speeds. With the prior Turin Zen 5c cores, AMD cut the L3 cache on each CCD in half and that allowed it to put more cores on the die but also crimped its performance on cache-sensitive workloads. This new approach seems sensible. Both the 12-core CCD, which has 48 MB of L3 cache, and the 32-core CCD, which has 128 MB of L3 cache, are etched using 2 nanometer processes from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

The other big change is that there are two different sockets, and both kinds of CCDs are used to make some of the CPU SKUs in both sockets.

The SP7 socket, which is shipping now and which makes heftier Venice processors, has a pair of I/O dies that deliver 16 channels of DDR5 memory that can deliver up to 1.6 TB/sec of bandwidth using MRDIMMs running at 12.8 GT/sec and 1 TB/sec using regular RDIMMs running at 8 GT/sec. Each channel can have one memory stick and they can be up to 512 GB in capacity. (If you think you can afford that. . . .) The SP7 socket has 96 PCI-Express 6.0 lanes running at 64 Gb/sec each with eight PCI-Express 4.0 lanes running at 16 Gb/sec; in a two socket configuration, 128 PCI-Express 6.0 lanes plus sixteen PCI-Express 4.0 lanes are exposed to the outside world and 64 of those PCI-Express lanes are used to make a NUMA link between a pair of CPU sockets.

This SP7 socket I/O (and memory) die is made using 6 nanometer processes from TSMC, just like the I/O (and memory) die for the Turin generation was, but this is clearly a different design. As we have pointed in the past, there is not a lot of benefit from using the most advanced processes to etch I/O and other signaling chiplets because I/O does not shrink as well as compute does. Such a shrink makes signaling more difficult and is also more expensive – two good reasons to hang back on the manufacturing process.

Here are the nine Venice chips that plug into the SP7 socket:

As we have done with past Epyc processors, we have calculated the relative performance of the Venice chips based on core count, clock speed, and improvement in instructions per clock (IPC) from generation to generation for integer workloads. This time around, the average performance uplift per core at the same clock speed for the Zen 6 core compared to the Zen 5 core, according to AMD, is 20 percent. This is a relatively big jump and is a testament to the core designers who are always coming up with new ways to get the core to do more work each cycle.

By the way, the Epyc 9G76 processor highlighted in blue font and red background in the SP7 socket processor table above is the one AMD has made specifically for the Helion AI racks. It is not particularly different from the Epyc 9686F chip aimed at HPC workloads, but I think they are distinct so they can be discounted differently. The hyperscalers and cloud builders are no doubt going to get better deals than the HPC centers of the world, given the high volumes they are purchasing.

Moving on to the SP8 socket, which is used for more mainstream Venice Epyc processors. And as such, it has only eight DDR5 memory channels per socket (four per I/O die) with two DIMMs per channel interleaving to boost capacity. The I/O die for the SP8 socket has 128 PCI-Express 6.0 lanes and eight bonus PCI-Express 4.0 lanes. So, half the memory bandwidth but 33 percent more I/O. In a two-socket NUMA setup, 64 PCI-Express 6.0 lanes are used to make the NUMA coherency and 192 lanes are exposed to the outside world plus those sixteen PCI-Express 4.0 bonus lanes. (That is for the pair of I/O dies, of course.)

AMD has confirmed to us that the SP8 I/O (and memory) die is etched with TSMC 6 nanometer processes, as we expected.

Here are the 22 variants of the Venice Epyc CPUs outfitted for the SP8 socket:

The SP8 socket versions of the Venice CPUs will not ship until next year, and it is my guess that it will happen fairly early in the year although officially all that AMD is saying is that they will ship sometime in the first half of 2027.

Comparisons Are Absolutely Not Odious

With that out of the way, lets see how the top bin parts and middle bin parts across the history of the Epyc line stack up in terms of performance and price/performance, and as usual we are using that Shanghai Opteron line as the baseline against which all comparisons are made. These were pretty much the last competitive Opterons that AMD shipped, which came out in the wake of the “Nehalem” Xeon 5500 chips where Intel copied an awful lot off of AMD’s homework and finally got a decent multicore chip out the door just as the Great Recession was starting and AMD was having issues with the Opterons.

Bad timing for AMD, good timing for Intel. But that is all ancient history now, and this time around AMD is not leaving any crack to exploit as AMD just keeps making better and better server CPUs and eats a little more market share with every passing quarter. It is a wonder that Intel has been able to hold onto the market share is does get, to be honest.

Let’s start with the top bin parts:

In these comparisons, I ignored the special HPC variants that AMD has shipped from time to time, which are denoted with a F designation for frequency optimized and an X designation of they have extra vertical cache on the package. So these are top bin standard parts.

Also, I put top bin parts in the comparison for both the SP7 and SP8 variants in the Venice lineup.

As is immediately obvious in the chart above, the relative performance of the top bin Epycs have scaled linearly, more or less, from the “Naples” Epyc 7001 series all the way through the Venice 9006 series with the SP8 socket. The SP7 socket with 256 cores is a total outlier in terms of the performance boost, and it takes the throughout performance up an exponential scale as you can see with your own eyes.

What also pops out instantly is how the bang for the buck of the first generation Naples processors improved compared to those Shanghai Opterons, but you have to remember that the gap in time is nine years – nine IT years where Moore’s Law was still available to boost performance and improve economics. (The Shanghai Opterons were etched in TSMC 45 nanometer processes, the Naples chips used GlobalFoundries 14 nanometer processes.)

What you can also see is how aggressively AMD moved in terms of price/performance with the “Rome” second generation Epycs, which is when the company first moved to distinct compute tiles and an I/O die linking them together and to the outside world. With the Milan Epycs, performance went up for the top bin part, but value for dollar improvement slowed and the same thing happened again with the fourth-gen “Genoa” top bin parts. But with the Turin and Now Venice parts, AMD is once again pushing the price/performance envelope, and it is particularly awarding customers who go with the throughput-oriented SP7 variants. AMD is charging a slight premium for the SP8 versions of Venice, which have half as many cores that run a little bit faster.

Clock speed is always going to come at a premium because that adds heat faster than increasing cores after a process shrink.

The net result is that the Epyc 9996 SP7 part has 190X more oomph than the Opteron 2393 SE, and if offers that performance at a cost per unit of performance that is 14.9X lower. For AMD, the benefit is that the chip costs 12.8X as much and companies are happy to pay for it for server consolidation and agentic AI and traditional HPC workloads. For the Venice Epyc 9746 SP8 chip, the performance jump compared to the Shanghai Opteron 2393 SE is 108.2X, the bang for the buck has improved by 10.8X, and the price per chip is 10X higher.

The curve for middle bin server CPUs from AMD looks similar if a little flatter in some ways:

But once again, the value for dollar with Venice is a lot better than it was compared across prior Epyc CPU generations.

AMD is not only keeping the heat on Intel. It is turning it up. And it has to if it is to compete against the Arm collective that is rising among the hyperscalers and cloud builders who account for half of the server market these days.

item.title: AMD Tunes Up CPUs For Agentic AI With “Venice” Epyc Processors
item.description:
The introduction of the ChatGPT chatbot by OpenAI in late 2022 supercharged the launch of of the GenAI era that shows only a few signs of slowing down, at least in the near term.

The Democratic “Blue Wave” in the recent midterm elections in the United States, which could introduce more regulation for the AI industry and become a drag on the datacenter building boom around the country, could tap the brakes, and the latest scandal involving Nvidia co-founder and chief executive officer Jensen Huang could be a blip on the screen or a longer-term issue. It’s hard to tell how this will shake out.

That said, the emerging agentic AI market is forecast to expand rapidly, with some analyst firms calling for it to grow almost 43 percent annually between now and 2034. Agentic AI also will drive a shift within datacenter infrastructure. Over the past four years, the various waves of generative AI like reasoning and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have been a boon for GPU makers – none more than Nvidia , which has seen its valuation soar into the trillions – and pushed the CPU, long the processor of choice for datacenter operators, into a supporting role.

But the computation demands of agentic AI are different from those of chattybot GenAI models froma few years back and require the capabilities that CPUs bring to the table for both AI host processors and AI sandboxes that run code generated by AI models.

In the agentic AI era, “the shape of the workload changes entirely,” Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager for compute and enterprise AI at AMD, wrote in May . “Instead of answering one prompt, an agent breaks a goal into steps, decides what to do next, calls multiple models, queries databases, connects with APIs, runs enterprise applications, checks permissions, retrieves memory, validates output and then loops back through the process again. It’s a very different infrastructure profile than prompt-in-answer-out chatbot AI.”

CPUs are better than GPUs at orchestrating the various complex AI agent tasks, as well as policy, security, and agent execution. That promises to change what’s needed in datacenter systems. Right now, the ratio of GPUs to CPUs is somewhere between 1:4 and 1:8. The expectation is that with agentic AI, that ratio will be brought to 1:1, more comfortable numbers for AMD, Intel, and other CPU makers.

That is a point AMD executives are making this week as the give more details about the 6 th Gen Epyc CPUs – formerly known as “Venice” – and the 6 th generation of the Zen microarchitecture. As Mike Clark, Corporate Fellow, senior vice president, and lead Zen architect at AMD, told journalists and analysts during recent briefing, “we didn't have a foresight that agentic was going to be what it has become, but we have always believed that the Core Complex Die was going to play a critical role in AI. We did a big investment in Zen 5 to do that, but with Zen 6, we continued to invest down that path and enhance our AI capability and it's paying off as agentic has taken off.”

As we’ve written before, agentic AI doesn’t mean that AMD will be able to chase down Nvidia in the still booming GPU market, but the company will continue to fair well against long-time CPU rival Intel – AMD’s share of the datacenter CPU market is about 46 percent – and most importantly, make a lot of money doing so.

The message from Madhu Rangarajan, corporate vice president for compute and enterprise AI products, during the call with journalists and analysts, was that the developments in the “Venice” sixth generation Epyc X86 CPUs that make them fit so well with the demands of agentic AI were a natural progression in the evolution of the server CPUs over the past eight years, since the introduction of the first generation “Naples” chips in 2018.

With the fourth generation “Genoa” CPUs in 2022, AMD began to expand its roadmap to serve multiple datacenter market segments, Rangarajan said.

“So with your Genoa and your Turin and your Bergamo and your Siena, you had your optimized design points going after different sub-segments of the market,” he said. “That's where we really started growing up to have a full portfolio of products here, and continued that.”

Rangarajan echoed Clark, saying he couldn’t claim that AMD purpose-built the Venice CPU family for agentic AI, but said the chips fit well with the needs of AI agents because they spend a broad set of workloads, adding that “we really now have a portfolio ready for the agentic AI era. We’ve got 1,000-plus instances, and what that allows customers to do is get a consistent offering, no matter how they want it to fly.”

With the Venice Epyc 9006 series chips, AMD is essentially doubling the throughput from one generation to the next, with the Venice chips delivering 1.9X the throughput of the prior “Turin” Epyc 9005 processors. The CPUs also measure up to throughput and per-core performance when compared to Nvidia’s Vera , Intel’s 6 th Gen Xeon 6980P , and Arm’s AGI processors.

Here’s the first comparison to Nvidia Vera:

And here is the comparison to Intel and Arm CPUs:

AMD is increasing the speed of the Venice chips, from 5.0 GHz with 64 cores with Turin to 5.3 GHz with 96 cores. Memory bandwidth jumps from 12 channels of DDR5 at 614 GB/sec to 16 channels at 1.6 TB/sec while I/O bandwidth doubles from PCI-Express Gen 5 to Gen 6, too.

Concurrent agents is an important measure these days, according to Rangarajan. AMD’s 6 th Gen 256-core chip at 400 watts offers 3.3 times the agents-per-watt that Nvidia’s Vera does, 1.8 times the agents-per-dollar compared with Intel’s 6 th Gen Xeons, and 1.5 times the agents per Helion AI Rack than fit in a Vera rack.

The Epyc 9006 chips also deliver better density and efficiency than Vera, according to AMD.

As AMD pushes its latest generation of CPUs into a hot agentic AI market, such numbers matter as the types of workloads expand, Rangarajan said.

“What agentic AI is doing is it's driving CPU demand across three networks vs. just general-purpose servers,” he said. “Agents like to do searches, in search clusters. Agents execute enterprise tools – CRM, ERP – we increasingly have agents doing EVM workloads. Your agents are accessing databases. All of this needs a broad CPU portfolio for these workloads.”

Rangarajan pointed to the pipeline of compute stages for agentic AI, noting that while the 192-core fifth generation Epyc 9965 from the Turin family outperformed Intel’s 128-core Xeon 6980P and Amazon’s 192-core Graviton5 chips, the 256-core Epyc 9996 Venice processor out performs them by greater margins.

He zeroed in on the performance with ephemeral tools, which are short-lived, isolated runtimes created during an agent session or task and are destroyed automatically.

“Ephemeral tools are the more interesting part of agentic AI because there is no well-defined benchmark there,” Rangarajan said. “It's a very, very, broad set of workloads. What we did was picked a few workloads – group graph, document parsing, coding agent, compilation – so we picked a big step we thought was representative of some of the agentic workloads we are seeing run inside of AMD. ... Overall, if you just break it down stage by stage in the pipeline, you're doing pretty well in each of the stages and the mix of these workflows could be different or different agentic workflows. But overall, we think we're doing well with Venice for agentic workloads.”

We have an analysis of the Venice SKU stack coming right up and will do an architectural deep dive on the Venice CPUs as well as what to expect from forthcoming "Verano" and "Venice-X" CPUs that are due next year. Stay tuned.

item.title: Datacenter Systems Spending To Go Through The Roof In 2027
item.description:
It was a rough couple of days for the datacenter business in the wake of the elections in the United States last week, but the optimism about the future will very likely continue unabated. Right up to the moment when it might not.

Just ahead of the election, the analysts and market researchers revised their IT spending forecast for 2026, which is damned near done now, and provided its first forecast for 2027, which looks like a killer year for IT spending. There are more than a few prognosticators who think that next year will be the peak and not because demand is not expected to be crazy after that but rather because there is a political uprising against tech titans and their datacenter and electricity needs at the same time that it was looking increasingly unlikely that electricity generation and distribution could be ramped up enough to meet datacenter demand in 2030, but less in 2028.

There is a lot that can and cannot happen in 2028, and it remains difficult to predict the future much further out than twelve to eighteen months out given the wonkiness and wobbliness of the data right now and in the near term, which drives the forecast further out.

That said, people make plans for their own IT spending based against the forecasts that IDC, Gartner, and others make, so it is important to be aware of how these forecasts change over time and how growth breaks down across the different segments of the IT economy.

Without further ado, here is the Gartner IT spending forecast for 2026 and 2027:

One new twist has been added with the November 2026 forecast, and it is a useful one. Gartner has extracted Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) cloudy compute, storage, and networking rentals out of the vast IT services segment as its own category. Now, we can see the revenues from the sale of datacenter systems (again: servers, storage, and networking hardware and their embedded operating systems software) as well as rental of such capacity.

Gartner only gave figures for 2026 and 2027 for this new category, but we can use the percent change to work out IaaS spending in 2025 and extract it out of the IT services spending. Moreover, if you scan the Internet, you can find Gartner IaaS spending figures from 2015 through 2024. I have added those to my monster table and made estimates of where IaaS spending was globally in 2012, 2013, and 2014 to complete the dataset. All of these figures were then extracted from the overall IT services figures we have compiled over more than a decade from Gartner so we can see the longer trend of spending for IaaS rentals and IT services without IaaS.

Take a gander:

Now that is a table. . . .

Here is the neat thing that immediately leaps out of this table to me: For the longest time, enterprise software revenues were 2X to 3X the size of datacenter systems sales. But the advent of truly ridiculously expensive AI systems and the huge amount of spending on them as well as the upgrades to back office (transactional) and front office (data analytics and customer engagement) systems that feed into the AI systems has the combined spending on datacenter systems plus IaaS surpassing enterprise software next year – $1.73 trillion for the hardware spending, up 48 percent year on year, compared to $1.68 trillion for enterprise software, up a very normal 14.7 percent.

The other neat bit is that spending on IT services minus IaaS will be in the same ballpark next year in Gartner’s forecast, up a more anemic 4.9 percent but still almost 2X as fast as global gross domestic product growth. It has been my contention after decades of watching IT spending trends that mature markets tend to grow at around 2X that of GDP.

For those of you who like to think visually, here is the trends for the segments of spending that together make up what I call core IT:

That’s systems, enterprise software, and services. For all the talk of Appmageddon or Softwaremageddon or what have you, as you can see enterprise software spending has been on a new binge level even before the coronavirus pandemic hit in March 2020, and it looks like it really got going for a new and steeper line starting around 2017. The enterprise software line is not steepening, like spending for datacenter systems has been doing. But as you can also plainly see, Gartner thinks that the growth rate for spending on datacenter systems is going to cool in 2027 to a mere 55.4 percent after an explosive 2026 where growth was 73.8 percent. The average growth rate for datacenter systems revenues between 2013 and 2021 inclusive was a mere 2.3 percent, which compared unfavorably to an average global GDP of 2.7 percent over the same time. The systems market was beyond mature until the pandemic hit and then GenAI exploded on the scene as we came out of it in 2022.

Core IT spending was not driven by servers, storage, and networking throughout most of this dataset – it was enterprise software and IT services that were in the driver’s seat and riding shotgun. Datacenter systems was in the trunk with duct tape over its mouth and zip ties on its hands and feet. (There’s an image for you. . . . ) The big change is that companies are becoming less stingy with the hardware budget because they can’t afford to miss the GenAI wave. In this regard, the GenAI boom most definitely resembles the Dot Com boom. But this time around, the hyperscalers and cloud builders already exist and they are hogging the allocations for GPUs and XPUs.

The world has changed so much in this decade and a half. Back in 2012, Core IT spending was a little more than a third of overall IT spending, and as 2027 comes to a close, Core IT will account for more than two thirds of the total. The resulting gap between global GDP growth and Core IT spending growth is not 2X, which is normal-ish, but more like 8X in 2026 and 7.3X in 2027, if the spending and the GDP figures pan out as Gartner and the World Bank expect, respectively.

We are not living in normal times, clearly.

Now, with a dataset that spans so many years, it is interesting to ponder how much of the increase in IT budget change is due to inflation and how much is due to capacity expansion. To get a feel for that, I have inflation adjusted the datacenter spending figures using the 2021 dollar as the fulcrum.

Now, this chart is just expressing currency inflation, not price inflation due to too much demand chasing too little supply. It is hard to say for sure, but it seems like about half the growth in datacenter systems spending this year is due to supply-demand issues, which drives up prices, and half is due to the increase in supply that chip and system makers can actually deliver to meet some of that demand. But that is just an educated guess.

This is just as bad as trying to buy plywood and two by fours or contractor services during the coronavirus pandemic. I know, because Nicole and I had to do major house repairs at that time and that was a very unfortunate time for that, let me assure you.

item.title: Google Rejiggers TPU Accelerators For Broader AI Inference Work
item.description:
Sometimes you need a new chip, and sometimes you need a new way to configure the chips you have to better suit the workloads you have. So it is with two new TPU accelerators that Google will be rolling out next year for its eponymous cloud and maybe even for some of its handful of direct customers who can get their hands on iron based on Google’s homegrown compute engines for their own datacenters.

To be specific, there are two new variants of the “Sunfish” TPU 8t and “Zebrafish” TPU 8i accelerators that Google first revealed back in April of this year . The TPU 8t is made at the behest of Google by Broadcom’s chip shepherding unit and is expected to be rolling into Google datacenters right now. The TPU 8i is being shepherded by MediaTek and earlier this year had experienced some delays; it is unclear if it is shipping to Google now or not. The modified versions of these Sunfish and Zebrafish systems are expected to be installed sometime in 2027, and we are optimistically predicting that this will start happening in Q1 2027 with ramping happening over the next year and a half until the machines are available in multiple Google Cloud regions around the globe. These ramps take time.

For instance, in the interim between the Sunfish and Zebrafish announcements in April and today, Google rolled out the predecessor “Ironwood” TPU v7p accelerators, which were first deployed in Q4 2025 for the company’s internal use, onto the Google Cloud and actually put pricing out for them in its US-Central1 region in Iowa and its Europe-West2 region outside London. My monster TPU table below has this updated pricing included. It took approximately a year for enough excess Ironwood capacity to be available that Google could put it out for rent on the cloud.

Let’s drill down into the new Sunfish and Zebrafish systems.

The TPU 8t was explicitly designed to run AI training workloads, and it supports Google’s 3D torus interconnect that spans 9,600 accelerators in a shared coherent memory space and that delivers a stunning 121 exaflops of oomph at FP4 precision. Each Sunfish 8i device has 216 GB of HBM3E memory across six stacks. This is by far the largest shared memory computing footprint in the AI space, and you can bet that Google wants as many TPU 8t accelerators as it can get out of Broadcom and chip foundry partner Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co so it can train up its Gemini frontier models.

On a conference call going over the new TPU machines, Mark Lohmeyer, vice president and general manager of AI and computing infrastructure at Google, said that these machines are organized into the 9.600-unit pods and then ganged up to create a cluster with over 1 million TPU 8t devices, and that such a cluster was indeed used to train the Gemini 4 Carbon frontier model that was delayed a bit and giving the company a certain amount of heartburn. Gemini 4 Carbon, developed by its DeepMind unit, was announced on October 28 . The Carbon model was delivered a few weeks after Gemini 4 Argon, and does better across the board. For API access through Google Cloud, both models have “an introductory price” of at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95 percent off input token price.

The TPU 8tx is a special variant of the TPU 8t that is really aimed at inference workloads (even though it can still do training during idle times) that has two major tweaks. The first is that the 3D torus interconnect on the TPU 8t has been replaced with the boardfly (a variant of dragonfly) interconnect that Google invented to create a more tightly coupled, lower latency interconnect suitable for inference workloads – particularly for complex agentic workloads that have many inference streams running at the same time. So the pod size drops from 9,600 accelerators down to 1,152 accelerators. Because the diameter of the fabric is 8.3X smaller, the network is flatter and the average latency through the resulting smaller system based on the boardfly topology (still using the same proprietary Inter Chip Interconnect, or ICI) is about half that of the 3D torus topology.

The other change with the TPU 8tx is that Google is switching out its own Axion Arm server CPU and replacing it with an unnamed AMD Epyc processor. The switch is being made because the AMD processors have on-board root of trust and encryption accelerators, which allows for workloads running on the TPU 8tx iron to remain encrypted right up to the point where it is being used and re-encrypted once processing on the TPUs is completed. Google has implied that it is a custom Arm Epyc part, but that could be more about core count and clock speed than anything else. It could be a current “Turin” Epyc 9005 or an impending “Venice” Epyc 9006 processor. Google has its own encryption and security processors, and the wonder is why this functionality is not already embedded into the TPU architecture and in the Axion processors. I would bet that with the TPU 9 family and the next-generation Axion CPUs it will be, so this could be a short-term victory for AMD.

With the TPU 8i Max, Google is focusing on larger context AI inference workloads, and to attack these, it is doubling up the number of Zebrafish accelerator complexes per socket. However, the amount of HBM memory capacity per socket is up only 33 percent compared to the original TPU 8i announced in April.

To be more precise, at a chip level, the original Zebrafish 8i chip had eight HBM3 (not higher bandwidth HBM3E) stacks with a total of 288 GB of capacity and 8.6 TB/sec of aggregate bandwidth. With the TPU 8i Max, there are two chips, but each has only 192 GB of capacity but the bandwidth per chip remains the same at 8.6 TB/sec. That means the number of HBM3 stacks is the same per Zebrafish chip, but the capacity per chip has been reduced by 33 percent. This implies a move from twelve-high HBM3 stacks to eight-high stacks. It also means there is less HBM memory per unit of compute with the TPU 8i Max versus the TPU 8i – even if the absolute memory per socket is higher. This looks like Google is spreading out its HBM3 memory allocation over more TPU chips, and tightly coupling two Zebrafish chips to make it have a bigger shared memory footprint for context and KV cache storage for inference models.

Everything in architecture is a tradeoff for something to trade up something else. This could leave some compute stranded, but that is not as bad as not having enough memory per socket to run large context. The wonder is that Google did not deprecate some of the compute to balance it back out – or have MediaTek and TSMC sort through the bins to find Zebrafish chips that had 33 percent lower oomph to balance out the memory. Go figure.

If you look carefully at the TPU 8i Max card, it looks like the ICI port at the bottom of the board is different from the other TPU 8 sockets. This has not been explained.

Here is the monster table that lines up all the feeds and speeds and pricing we know for the TPU compute engines:

What remains to be seen is how Google will price the Sunfish and Zebrafish TPUs.

It is reasonable to expect for Google to charge a premium for TPUs that are used for training since the elasticity of the GenAI market depends on ever-decreasing costs of chewing on and spitting out tokens for inference runs. It seems likely that the TPU 8t will be more expensive per flops and per HBM capacity than the TPU 8i, with the TPU 8tx carrying a slight premium per hour over the TPU 8t and TPU 8i and the TPU 8i Max costing a little less than 2X that of the TPU 8i per hour.

One last thing. Google has created a hierarchical storage management software layer that rides atop TPUs called TPU Sync that is designed to maximize HBM memory use while sporadic and bursty agentic AI workloads are running.

“What this means is that TPUs are actually often idle a large percentage of the time,” explained Lohmeyer. “And so if you were to have to keep those resources tied up even when they are not being used, that creates huge inefficiencies, especially as these agentic workloads really start to scale. So this is exactly what TPU Sync is designed to address.”

“The way it works is it moves the working memory off the TPU chip when an agent pauses, and then restores it when the agent needs to resume processing. This significantly drives up the utilization of the system because when we free up those accelerated resources, we can apply them to some other task. So you can take the utilization up significantly, and that ultimately drives down the cost per transaction, the cost per agentic workload or activity. So it's really key to the one of the core value props of TPU is driving great performance at the lowest possible cost.”

And because TPU Sync is software, Google can back cast it to earlier generations of TPU systems, and it has indeed done just that. So the TPU 5, TPU 6, TPU 7 and TPU 8. It is not at all clear how TPU Sync can orchestrate memory movement across tens of thousands to millions of TPUs in a cluster. The chart above does not, in my mind, really convey how data must move back and forth across HBM, host DRAM, host flash, and external flash and disk storage, but clearly this must be done. It is also not clear how much TPU Sync boosts inference throughput. I look forward to seeing such data.

item.title: IBM, AMD, And Oak Ridge Unveil Quantum Error Correction Platform
item.description:
Over the past few years, quantum computing companies have made remarkable strides in addressing the central challenge of correcting errors the systems make, a hurdle that needs to be cleared before practical, commercial fault-tolerant quantum computing can fully be realized.

We have written about a range of approaches to error correction that are being worked on, from running an error-correction code with a quantum processing unit (QPU) created with a different grid to using a decoder that can run on a single CPU to leveraging AI reinforcement learning .

Each effort is made to reach the same basic goals, including reducing the number of errors quantum systems make and lowering the technical overhead needed to make this happen to help them scale and keep the costs down. Logical qubits – the group of many physical qubits – is a key technique for reducing errors, but more needs to be done. Quantum systems typically now have gate error rates ranging from one error per 100 to 1,000 operations. The error rate needs to improve significantly for fault-tolerant systems to become a reality.

The problem is that qubits are extremely fragile and can fall apart – or decohere – and lose their quantum nature through noise, which can range from light and sound to the activity of other qubits.

IBM, AMD, and the Quantum Science Center at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory this week unveiled a co-design platform for error correction (below) that integrates quantum computing with classical HPC systems and, importantly, puts the systems next to each other in the same location. This rarely happens, according to IBM, which means that connectivity needs to be made through the cloud with the help of APIs, with can lead to greater complexity and delays.

“In order to experiment with these techniques and build algorithms, quantum and classical processors need to be able to work closely together,” Seetharami Seelam, Distinguished Engineer and chief architect of classical system co-design for quantum-centric supercomputing, tells The Next Platform .

Quantum systems will work closely with traditional supercomputers in hybrid, quantum-classical environments, with quantum processing units (QPUs) essentially acting as another accelerator, alongside GPUs, TPUs, and other chips. AI will work as a connective tissue between the systems, with a lot of work being done – including by Oak Ridge scientists – to determine the roles generative and agentic AI will have in these environments.

“The collaboration will also focus on exploring how AI can develop more effective algorithms and workflows, as well as advancing error correction through both new methods and improvements to existing approaches,” Seelam says. “The GPUs that are part of the co-design platform will play a key role in running the AI models or algorithms that scientists plan to develop and improve upon.”

The co-design platform will be housed at IBM’s facility in Poughkeepsie, New York, and include IBM quantum computers, in particular the company’s 120-bit Nighthawk r2 quantum chip and Oak Ridge’s Umbra HPC system (below), which is powered by AMD’s fifth generation Epyc “Turin” Epyc 9005 datacenter CPUs and “Antares” Instinct MI355X GPUs . The AMD chips will power the classical system’s research into quantum error correction, decoding optimization, and software orchestration, according to the organizations.

Researchers will be able to use the tightly integrated platform to test and develop quantum-classical workflows, test quantum algorithms, and learn more about what error-corrected systems will need without having to pull together the infrastructure themselves. The goal is to use the platform as a jumping-off point for creating quantum systems and software in the years ahead.

IBM officials put an emphasis on Nighthawk’s square lattice connectivity, a change from Big Blue’s previous “heavy-hex”-based chip architecture. Square lattice connectivity offers a two-dimensional grid topology where most qubits connect directly to four nearest neighbors, about a 60 percent increase in connectivity over heavy-hex. It also leads to shorter execution times and compatibility with standard surface code for error correction. Combined high speed in maximum circuits per second and real-time pulse control, researchers will be able to better test error correction techniques and compare them in terms of qubits, time, and classical compute resources to get a better handle how GPUs can best facilitate quantum computing.

Through IBM’s quantum API, researchers can access deep pulse capabilities that will allow them to measure qubits mid-calculation and then deal with the results in real time, including set the exact timing of signals that can protect qubits from noise.

IBM pointed to hierarchical error correction as an example of what can be further explored with the platform. With the hierarchical approached, two codes are layered together. One is an inner code for protecting qubits within a module, with the other an outer code adding a second layer of protection. An advantage is that this approach keeps the hardware and connectivity demands simpler. According to IBM research, the approach could reach a trillion logical operations at a physical qubit error rate of one in 1,000.

It also relies on classical computing, and the platform will let researchers use GPUs to test such idea in an environment with low latency.

It also dovetails with the goal set by the US Energy Department’s Quantum Genesis Mission for developing fault-tolerant quantum systems. IBM, in conjunction with the University of Chicago, in July demonstrated experiments that involved up to 70 logical qubits and 438 hard operations, according to IBM’s Seelam.

“The Quantum Genesis Mission’s Q Competition targets 100 logical qubits running 100,000 such operations by late 2028,” he says. “To reach this goal, the broader quantum community needs to achieve a 238-fold increase in hard operation count, and we need to do it fast. We believe this goal is feasible, but achieving it will require progress across several areas and close collaboration among industry, national laboratories and government researchers.”

The tightly integrated quantum-classical platform will offer the resources needed to test systems to reach the Genesis Mission goal, Seelam says.

IBM also will take advantage of the work done on the platform as it develops its Quantum Starling system, which the company says will be a fault-tolerant computer that is expected to be delivered by 2029.

item.title: Arista Lines Up Networking For 10 Gigawatts Of AI Systems
item.description:
It takes a while to tame a new computing architecture, and so it is understandable that the AI-related ramp at all Ethernet switch makers – and particularly at arch rivals Cisco Systems and Arista Networks – has taken many years to come to fruition. And, to be frank, they are all just getting started.

It is not just a matter of making higher bandwidth Ethernet switches and riding down the cost per bit flitted curves as the aggregate bandwidth per ASIC doubles and the cost of moving bits goes down a little, allowing for elastic consumption and larger and larger networks to balance out larger and larger clusters. That would be relatively easy, and pretty much defines the cloud networking era from 2010 through 2020.

AI is different. It demands high radix devices and flatter networks because the workload is inherently latency sensitive, and given the extremely high cost of a GPU or XPU relative to other kinds of compute, keeping these compute engines waiting is economically devastating. If GPUs and XPUs were “cheap as chips,” an English phrase referring to the friend potatoes that accompany fried fish in pub food, we would tolerate some inefficiencies and interleave workloads across more devices and make it up in volume. That is not an option when it comes to AI training or AI inference – hasn’t been for years and won’t ever be again. The tokenomics will kill the goose that lays the golden trillions of tokens otherwise.

Moreover, AI requires AI. To balance workloads across tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of accelerators in a datacenter or region and across millions of accelerators across regions requires all kinds of dynamic routing and switching and the processing of untold amounts of telemetry. Keeping these accelerators business means embedding AI into management tools, like Arista’s Autonomous Virtual Assistant, because human beings cannot correlate and analyze data at the pace of computers. Securing this infrastructure also requires AI because bad actors are also using AI to find vulnerabilities and exploit them. All of this development has also taken time.

The Inevitability Of Ethernet

No one – not hyperscalers, not cloud builders, not AI model builders, not national HPC labs, not sovereigns, not AMD – except Nvidia wants proprietary networks anywhere in the interconnect hierarchy for AI clusters. And Nvidia got out way ahead of everyone else in creating tightly coupled, shared memory GPU clusters and deserves its first mover advantages when it comes to market share, revenue, and profits. But, as I have pointed out, NVSwitch and NVLink are the InfiniBand of scale up and scale in networking and they will have to compete against more open – and presumably cheaper – alternatives based on Ethernet running ESUN or UALink protocols and perhaps native UALink for gluing GPU memories together and UCI-Express for gluing components together within an accelerator package.

But this transition is going to take time. At the moment, Arista Networks is making money selling Ethernet switches for regular cloudy infrastructure and for AI front ends – the networks that connect AI clusters to the outside world and storage. The company is also making serious money peddling its R series Ethernet switches that are augmented with routing functions to do scale across datacenter linkages, which is used to make AI clusters span multiple datacenters and regions. This is necessary because you can only build a datacenter or region so big because power is often limited in a given geographic area. The hyperscalers and cloud builders have to spread it around.

Arista has yet to make any serious money selling Ethernet switchery for scale up networks (also called the AI back end by some), but there are some trials that have been under way at the hyperscalers and cloud builders to run the ESUN and UALink over Ethernet (UALoE) protocols atop Ethernet fabrics.

On a call with Wall Street analysts going over the company’s third quarter financial results, Jayshree Ullal, Arista’s chief executive officer, said that the company has worked with AMD, Arm, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, and Qualcomm on rackscale switching based on its Etherlink switching and routing lines, and added that she expected for scale up trails based on the ESUN protocol to start in 2027, initially with rackscale systems with a radix of 128 or 144 accelerators within a rack and with as many as 1,000 accelerators across a row. (The number is almost certainly 1,024 accelerators, not 1,000, and she was speaking generally.) Production rollouts for ESUN scale up networks are not expected until 2028.

This seems like a long time away, and the wonder is what is taking so long.

Arista has not said it will embrace UALink switching, which will more directly competes against Nvidia’s NVSwitch stack, but that is always a possibility given the availability of third party UALink ASICs from Astera Labs, Marvell, Upscale AI, and maybe Panmnesia.

Arista does not really have a play for scale in networking down on AI accelerator packages. That is something for AMD, Nvidia, Broadcom, Marvell, Alchip, and maybe Intel and Qualcomm to do.

Before scale up ramps, there is plenty of money to be made peddling scale across and scale out networking for now, as Arista’s third quarter results show.

You can finally see the beginning of the proverbial hockey stick curve driven by GenAI in the product revenue curve shown above. Arista has been waiting years for that to happen.

In the September quarter, Arista posted product sales of $3.19 billion, up 66.9 percent year on year and up 22.4 percent sequentially. Services revenues plug along behind that, as always, and grew by 17.9 percent to $467.6 million in the quarter.

Add it up, and total revenues for Q3 came to $3.66 billion, up 58.5 percent, and sequential growth was 20.5 percent overall. This is 2X to 3X higher sequential growth than is normal and is the highest level set by the company since its founding years. (Which almost don’t count because there are so few deals and so little money comparatively back in the beginning of a company.)

Arista’s operating income was $1.64 billion, up 67.9 percent, and its net income was $1.56 billion, up 82.9 percent. That net income is a very healthy 42.7 percent of revenues, and it is the highest level of profits the company has ever enjoyed. The company exited Q3 with $14.36 billion in cash and equivalents and had $11.4 billion in customer purchase commitments and $6.84 billion in deferred revenues, also very healthy relative to the size of the business.

Ullal gave us some numbers that allow us to update our annual Arista product segment model, which is shown below forecasting 2026 and 2027:

And here is the same data shown graphically so you can feel the curves:

On the call, Ullal said that Arista was on track to sell about $3.5 billion in AI front end and back end networking gear and services in 2026 and that this would double to $7 billion or so in 2027. Campus switching, which is an easy adjacency that helps take money away from Cisco and others, would hit $1.25 billion this year and grow to $2 billion next year. At the midpoint of growth targets, Arista will grow overall revenues by 52 percent in 2026 to hit $13.3 billion and will grow by another 39.1 percent in 2027 to reach $18.5 billion.

We have to guess how the non-AI and campus portions of the Arista business will do, and gave it our best shot in the table and chart above. The portions of the business not relating to AI front end and back end networks (which does include scale across networking linking datacenters and regions) are growing well in 2026, mostly thanks to that scale across gear that is in the routing product segment. The core cloud and datacenter switching business and the edge segment are growing, but not by much. I see this dichotomy in servers, too. Traditional workloads are growing more in servers, in fact, than they are in switching. This could yet change.

Also looking ahead, Ullal said that its current customers that account for 10 percent or more of annual revenue – that would be Microsoft and Meta Platforms – are working with Arista on ESUN scale up networks for their respective Maia and MTIA XPUs and are still on track to be big spenders in 2026 and 2027. She added that the company might add one or perhaps two more big spenders in the coming year, which is fueling its growth in 2027 presumably.

The market is inflecting, hard. In 2024 and 2025, said Ullal, Arista was talking about having four or five customers with AI clusters in the range of 50,000 to 100,000 Nvidia GPUs, and seeing a lot of InfiniBand still going into machines. Here in 2026, Arista already has more than a hundred customers using its AI-centric Etherlink switches, and by the end of 2027, she is forecasting that the company will provide networking for 10 gigawatts of AI cluster capacity and will be linking ten or more different kinds of accelerators.

item.title: AMD Cannot Catch Nvidia, But It Sure Can Make Some Money
item.description:
Capitalism requires strong competition to function properly, and because of that, I have always been enthusiastic about the clash of vendors and economic and technical substitution, which is not just a good idea but a law of economics.

I have watched the rise of GPU compute at Nvidia from the beginning, I have watched AMD fumble and stumble and eventually become credible in datacenter CPUs (for the second time) and in datacenter GPU accelerators (for the first time with the Instinct MI200 series).

But let’s be honest. AMD is hurting Intel, which has no datacenter GPU or indeed any AI accelerator to speak of, a hell of a lot more than it is hurting Nvidia. And that, I think, is mostly because AMD cannot make more Instinct GPUs because it cannot get more HBM allocations from Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. And to be perfectly frank, AMD is selling even fewer GPUs than it otherwise might because it is loading up the HBM memory on the Instinct MI400 series a lot more than is Nvidia with its “Blackwell” B200s and B300s and its “Rubin” R200s to get a more fair balance of compute and memory capacity.

I would argue that the Instinct MI500 series should have optical interposers and put disaggregated and composable HBM memory on trays adjacent to and interconnected with GPU accelerators, allowing for memory to be recycled and conserved as the GPU engines are swapped out with increasing capabilities, and that if AMD did this, it could have an intense architectural advantage over what Nvidia brings to market with static configurations that are intentionally under-memoried to ramp up GPU accelerator volumes. I doubt such a thing will happen, but it would be wonderful to see. Given the insane cost of DRAM in general, I wish the same thing for the future “Florence” Zen7 series of Epyc datacenter CPUs – trays of disaggregated and composable CPUs and DRAM banks so the DRAM can live on without having to throw it away as CPUs change.

No one is expecting such a thing as far as I know, and that is one reason why AMD is not really taking market share away from Nvidia in datacenter GPUs. And AMD is taking share from Intel in datacenter CPUs not only because it has designed a superior X86 product, but because it has taken care of its process nodes and supply chain of packaging and can actually grow its X86 shipments faster than Intel – and do so at a higher average selling price. We don’t have third quarter market share numbers as yet, but generally speaking, AMD has a little more than a third of X86 server CPU shipments and a little less than half of revenues for the first half of 2026.

The gap between Nvidia and AMD is growing, not shrinking, and is expected to get even wider. To keep the comparison simple, I am going to just use top line revenue across all products, which makes AMD look stronger than it is against Nvidia because of its very good client CPU and GPU businesses. But you will get the point.

In 2021, a year before the GenAI boom started with the emergence of a practical and usable ChatGPT chatbot API, Nvidia had $26.9 billion in sales and AMD had $16.4 billion, a gap of 1.64X in favor of Nvidia. GPU computing had been in the market for a decade and a half, so it was not like this was new. AMD was just finding its footing architecturally. In 2023, Nvidia started pulling even more ahead, with its nearly $60.9 billion in sales being 2.69X larger than the $22.7 billion that AMD took in, which was helped by the coronavirus pandemic PC buying boom. This year, thanks to the GenAI boom, even with all of its efforts and in part because AMD does not own the most lucrative parts of the networking for AI (scale across, scale out, and scale up networking), Nvidia is going to have somewhere on the order of $354 billion in sales, which will be 6.79X higher than the $52.2 billion that AMD might bring in. And three years hence, as Marvell was showing off in its charts justifying its $115 billion acquisition of optical component supplier Lumentum yesterday , one set of Wall Street consensus estimates has Nvidia raking in $1,091 billion in calendar 2029 compared to $164 billion for AMD – a gap of 6.65X, essentially unchanged from today.

Genetics is not destiny, and neither is forecasting, of course. But you can see that AMD cannot get enough HBM to make a dent in the Nvidia datacenter GPU business. So AMD will do what is sensible, and that is to make money on what it can manufacture, and that is just fine because the AI market is not really competitive as much as it is underserved, which always gives pricing power to the vendors. Which is why we see all of the hyperscalers and cloud builders, as well as some of the big AI model builders, designing and having manufactured their own compute engines, which are cheaper and more specialized.

With all that as a backdrop, let’s focus on AMD’s financial results for the third quarter of 2026, when its two variants of its “Helios” AI rackscale systems – one with CPUs for agentic AI sandboxes, and the other with a mix of Epyc CPUs and Instinct GPUs for AI training and inference – were ramping production.

In Q3, AMD’s revenues were up 44.7 percent to $13.38 billion, and operating income was up by a factor of 2.2X to $2.83 billion as some of the costs for that Helion platform had been absorbed in prior quarters and as profits from the sales of components that go into these racks (which are made by OEMs and ODMs, not by AMD itself) started to rise. Net income was up 95.3 percent to $2.43 billion, which is 18.2 percent of revenues. AMD is inherently a lot less profitable than Nvidia, and sort of has to be, but these are nonetheless very good net margins for AMD.

The company’s cash hoard more than doubled year on year to $15.78 billion. It now has more than one quarter’s worth of revenue in the bank, which is a kind of security AMD has rarely experienced. This is a very healthy business in a cut-throat set of markets with very high production costs.

Two thirds of AMD’s revenues in the quarter came from datacenter products, which includes Epyc CPUs, Instinct GPUs, Pensando DPUs, and a few other things like Helios rack designs and ROCm software.

Data Center group revenues were $8.55 billion, up 96.9 percent and above the target growth rate of “more than 80 percent” that the company espoused a few months ago. Data Center group operating oncome was up by 2.7X to $2.88 billion, and comprising 33.7 percent of revenues.

AMD’s Client group, which sells CPUs and GPUs for PCs, had $2.95 billion in sales, up a mere 7.2 percent, and in my model, operating income was down 18.8 percent to $401 million.

Gaming revenues – which means discrete Radeon GPUs aimed at gamers – brought in another $773 million, down 40.4 percent, which would be a crisis only a few years ago but it is now noise in AMD’s data. My best guess is that Gaming group operating income was $172 million, down 53.9 percent. (Why AMD consolidates profits for Client and Gaming but breaks out revenues for these two groups is beyond me. Why make us guess?)

Embedded revenues – meaning Xilinx FPGAs – drove $1.11 billion in sales, up 29.4 percent. Operating income here rose by 60.1 percent to $453 million. That is three times the profitability of the PC chip business for the company.

In the Data Center group, it was once again, for the third quarter in a row, the CPUs that drove the majority of revenues. We have to back into that to put some numbers on it.

On the call with Wall Street analysts, AMD chief executive officer Lisa Su said that sales of Epyc server CPUs to hyperscalers and cloud builders “more than doubled,” and so did sales of CPUs that would end up in servers aimed at enterprise, telco, service provider, government, and academic institutions. When I plug that into my model, taking a stab at what “more than doubled” might mean in each case, I think hyperscaler and cloud builder CPU sales were up 2.2X to $3.53 billion while the enterprise et al segment saw a 105 percent increase to $1.15 billion. That yields total Epyc CPU sales of $4.68 billion, up 116 percent year on year.

If you make some assumptions about how much AMD made selling Pensando DPUs and other NICs and datacenter-class FPGAs (very much noise in the data) plus components for CPU and GPU system boards, that means Instinct GPU sales came in at $3.43 billion, up 72.3 percent. If AMD had 5X times the memory allocations and could line up the packaging for more GPUs, do I think it could sell them? Abso-freaking-lutely . Could it sell 10X that amount? Quite possibly . The fact that AMD did not make that revenue tells you how the HBM allocations are shaking out.
