Qualcomm executives this summer introduced an architecture called high-bandwidth computing (HBC), the solution to an ongoing problem in AI inferencing – and now in agentic AI – that they and others call the memory wall . Essentially, the performance of these models increasingly depends less on the compute capability of a processor – how fast the chip can calculate – and more on how quickly the chip can feed data to the calculation.

It’s an issue that affects both the performance of the AI model as well as the cost for running the AI workloads. Qualcomm outlined two strategies that are widely used – one that houses the AI model in fast on-chip memory, and another that uses stacked high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to support a processor. Qualcomm advocates a third strategy – near-memory computing, or HBC – that moves the computer closers to the all-important memory .

Executives argue that to close a widening gap – to remove the memory wall – between the need for more compute and the ability to feed that demand with data, the compute needs to move closer to the memory and the data it holds. It gives the AI model faster access to the data it needs, and reduces the time, energy, and cost that come when the data needs to travel a longer distance to get to the compute.

It’s an argument Qualcomm made in July when first pitching the HBC architecture, and one they continue to make now.

“In traditional computer architecture, you usually have DDR, you have memory of package, you have usually plenty of capacity on that, but you have a narrow link, which moves the data very slowly,” Gerardo Giaretta, vice president and general manager of datacenter CPU and AI at Qualcomm, recently told journalists and analysts. “So far, AI has been really focusing on the HBM architecture. It basically increases the number of lanes and how fast you can move the data between the compute and the HBM. The challenge with that is the premium you're going to pay for HBM, a premium in terms of the cost of the solution that goes in particular on the amount of power that HBM consumes and a complex interposer and 2.5D packaging, co-host packaging and so forth.”

That moving of the data to the compute side of things and back is the problem HBC – moving the compute next to where the data is stored – is solving, Giaretta argued.

“You have in-package, you have a stack of memory – in our case, LPDDR-based – and you have a compute die under the stack of memory,” he said. “Basically, you don't have to move the data anymore [in] packets. You automatically have a very, very high bandwidth between the memory and the compute and you have strong energy savings simply because now you're not moving data across millimeters, but you're moving data or across micrometers. Simply, the amount of space that the data traverses is much less, and that results in much better energy consumption as well as energy efficiency.”

Diving a bit deeper, Giaretta said in the first generation of HBC, Qualcomm uses the LPDDR stack and a full AI accelerator under the stack, where most of the operations for the AI workloads are done. Some operations may move to the central system-on-a-chip (SOC) – which is the vendor’s Dragonfly AI250 – depending on the architecture and its implementation. That said, most of the processing stays within the HBC package.

The AI250 – Qualcomm has started production of the AI inference platform, which is due for release next year – has significantly more TFLOPs, and the interface between the AI250 and LPDDR is slower than HBC. The key is to instruct the HBC to do what it needs to do, he said,

“ You should think about HPC in that particular implementation as a co-processor, as a coexistent,” Giaretta said. “Once you instruct that, and the majority of the decode operations are done within HBC, then your end-to-end performance is not affected by this slower link, because you just send back results. You don't have to send the data, you just have to send the results."

Since July, Qualcomm experts have been outlining the inferencing challenges that HBC will address. This week, the company announced that it now has first-generation HBC silicon in the lab, with its complete memory read-write path and near-memory computations at production levels validated in tests.

Qualcomm engineers used industry-standard automated test equipment (ATE) for the validation efforts. What the testing found is that HBC can deliver as much as 18 times the memory bandwidth vs. LPDDR, and an energy-efficiency measurement of five times the terabit-per-second-per-watt compared to HBM4, the sixth-generation of high-bandwidth memory.

“You can really do inference, and it drives a clear performance advantage on the solution,” Giaretta said of the results. “As we said at the beginning, AI inference is not only – but for the majority part – memory bandwidth-bound limited. This solution gives you the bandwidth that you need at the lowest energy. ... From an OPEX perspective, the energy efficiency – really the amount of energy that you spend moving the data – is at least one order of magnitude less.”

With the results in hand, Qualcomm is moving forward with its plans. Qualcomm for more than a year has been playing out plans to become a larger player in the AI datacenter space and an alternative to Nvidia . Now HBC will be integrated into Dragonfly AI250 to create what executives say will be a full AI inference accelerator platform, which will be foundational to the Qualcomm Dragonfly Rack, the vendor’s full stack infrastructure for inference workloads. The AI250 is expected to start sampling in the first half of 2027.

The validation of the HBC silicon also is the first step of a multi-year roadmap, with the sampling of the AI250 and the upcoming Dragonfly C1000 CPUs both set for next year and samples of the Dragonfly AI300 coming in 2028.

The validation “is particularly important for us because HBC is a clear differentiator of our solution versus others,” Giaretta said. “Our solution is not just memory. That's why we call it HBC, high-bandwidth compute. We have compute, with the real TFLOPs under the memory stack. Our solution is not just improving the memory bandwidth. Our solution is putting the compute just under the memory so that you have better memory bandwidth.”

He also noted that Qualcomm is working with various partners to determine the different ways HBC can be used. The Dragonfly AI250 isn’t the only products where it will be used.

The validation of the HBC silicon also should erase doubts about whether Qualcomm can keep its promise of high-yield manufacturing of the AI250 next year, he said.

“I's important to understand that this is not a normal chip,” Giaretta said. “This is the first time that somebody has done something like this. We usually don't do a blog or a pre-briefing and so forth for a bring-up of a chip. We do gazillions of chips in Qualcomm and we don't do that. The reason why we decided to do that is exactly because it's completely new technology and it's a good validation of what we will see next year in terms of high-yield manufacturing.” ®

item.title: AI Arms Race Puts Sovereign Supply Chains in the Spotlight
item.description:
During the Cold War, developing the atomic bomb was the first step toward building even more powerful nuclear weapons. That same logic now applies to the AI arms race. For nations like South Korea in particular, having the most powerful AI accelerator is secondary to having one that is domestically sourced or manufactured and eliminating its dependency on the US.

And, yes, as a longtime ally of the United States, South Korea can import as many GPUs from Nvidia or AMD as it pleases. But just because it can doesn't mean the nation is okay relying on America's often capricious government.

As we've seen repeatedly over the last few years, what Uncle Sam giveth can be taken away with little or no warning, and South Korea seems to be well aware of this fact.

The nation as it were is in a unique position to blaze its own AI infrastructure trail. The country is home to two of the world's largest memory vendors, SK Hynix and Samsung, giving domestic chip designers an advantage in securing HBM capacity. Samsung Electronics also happens to be the second largest leading edge wafer fab in the world, while Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co and Japan's Rapidus are just a short hop away.

As such, we've seen a handful of credible South Korean chip startups come and go since the start of the AI boom. FuriosaAI and Rebellions are the two frontrunners. There was also Sapeon for a hot minute, but its IP and talent were rolled into Rebellions back in late 2024.

Both companies have produced working silicon, which is more than a lot of chip startups can say, though their latest releases aren't exactly the most sophisticated.

Rebellions' Rebel100 accelerator, for example, first turned up in late 2025 , is roughly on par with Nvidia's three-year-old H200. Meanwhile, Furiosa's RNGD accelerator, which we looked at back in mid-2025, isn't even that powerful, delivering about 2.25x the performance per watt of Nvidia's now six-year-old A100 in the tested workloads.

But as we've seen with China's domestic AI infrastructure push, the chips don't need to be that fast if you've got enough of them. Having proven their designs, Rebellions and Furiosa are now working to advance new systems and next-gen chips.

This week, Furiosa announced a $620 million Series D funding round to scale production of its RNGD accelerators and continue development of its third-gen accelerators, which it's building in collaboration with Broadcom.

Furiosa expects to produce around 20,000 RNGD accelerators this year and roughly double that in 2027. To no one's surprise, Samsung and LG Electronics are among the company's biggest patrons.

We don't have a lot of info on Furiosa's next accelerator, but we do know it'll be fabbed on a 2 nm process (presumably TSMC's), use a multi-die chiplet architecture, and incorporate HBM4 or HBM4e depending on timing.

Broadcom's involvement in the chip's development points to a rack-scale architecture using something like Tomahawk 6 or Tomahawk Ultra and/or 3.5D XDSiP for package design.

3.5D XDSiP is an advanced packaging reference architecture designed by Broadcom as a shortcut for XPU designers to bring AMD Instinct-style accelerators to the market faster. From what we can tell, Meta and OpenAI have notably adopted the tech for their respective XPU platforms.

We don't know for sure that's what Furiosa is doing, but from what it has disclosed previously, it sure looks like a combination of the two. In any case, the move to a 2 nm process and HBM4 or 4e points to a significantly more potent accelerator.

The desire for sovereign AI — that is, AI trained and run on accelerators you own in datacenters within your nation's borders — isn't a phenomenon unique to South Korea. Neither is the desire to diversify supply chains on the off chance the arms race turns into a second cold war and Washington and Beijing start gatekeeping their best hardware.

We've already seen the mess the Trump administration caused trying to cut off China's access to Nvidia's H20 accelerators last year. That decision was quickly reversed, but not before Beijing got the message that US chip designers couldn't be counted on any longer.

As such, we've seen growing interest in alternative accelerators across EMEA and the Asia-Pacific regions. Japanese neocloud ai&, for example, recently announced plans to deploy up to 100 of Rebellions' RebelRack systems to support its GPU-based compute offering. For reference, that works out to 3,200 Rebel100 accelerators. It's not a huge win compared to the volumes of Blackwell or Instinct accelerators Nvidia and AMD ship each quarter, but it's something.

Meanwhile, Furiosa is cashing in on the dearth of competent European AI accelerators. This summer, the chip biz landed a deal with Equinix to field its RNGD accelerators at the colo's LS2 facility in Lisbon.

Rebellions and Furiosa may not have the most potent chips, but the simple fact that they're not American is enough to make them attractive for those looking to insulate their AI investments against supply chain disruptions.

item.title: SPONSORED: How to Evaluate CPU Performance for Agentic AI
item.description:
A funny thing happened on the way from machine learning to chatbots to agentic AI: the central processing unit, or CPU, that has dominated commercial computing for six decades and that was temporarily supplanted by GPUs and XPUs that are massively parallel and therefore very good at crunching lots of vector and matrix math, became central again. So much so that the CPU market is expected to grow from $26 billion in 2025 to $246 billion only five years later , with the bulk of that growth coming from AI host CPUs and agentic AI sandboxes for executing work as part of an agentic AI workflow.

But here’s the rub: not all CPUs are created equal, and hyperscalers, cloud builders, and AI model builders as well as neoclouds, sovereign AI centers, and enterprises are going to have to balance a desire to restrict the number of different CPU SKUs in their fleet against an equally strong desire to get a perfect match between different parts of the enterprise workflow that now includes agentic AI and the underlying hardware that supports all of those distinct pieces of human-written and AI-generated code that embodies their workflows.

And let’s not forget that the inference that underpins agentic AI is itself changing very fast.

This makes shopping for CPUs more complex than we have seen in the past with ever more complex workloads in the datacenter. At datacenter scale, the question becomes how many successful tasks can be completed within a rack’s power and thermal envelope. That is why Arm is advocating that customers must examine the performance of CPUs at the socket, the system, and the rack level, with an eye on both single thread performance of a CPU core and the scaling of cores within a socket, across a system, and spanning a rack to aggregate performance that can be used to run many AI agents concurrently while meeting the SLAs.

This is not the first time that the IT industry has had to deal with complex multi-tier, multi-system workloads and tried to create benchmark tests to simulate that complexity so companies could make intelligent purchasing decisions. The TPC-E benchmark, for instance, simulated the workings of a warehouse – the real kind, with forklifts, not a data warehouse – and had a mix of interactive and batch workloads running across database, application, and infrastructure tiers.

“Multi-tier and stateful computing are not new, and existing cloud and enterprise benchmarks remain important for understanding individual parts of the system,” Jeff Defilippi, Senior Director, Product Management at Arm, tells The Next Platform . “What changes with agentic AI is how those components are composed. A single task can dynamically chain model calls, retrieval, database transactions, code execution, tool invocations and state changes, with the result of one step determining what happens next. That makes successful task completion, not any single component metric, the more meaningful unit of performance.”

“So that does not make existing benchmarks less useful. We still need component-level measurements to understand where performance differences come from,” Defilippi continues.  “But they need to be connected to end-to-end measurements that show how quickly and efficiently the system completes the task, and how that performance holds up as more agents run concurrently and the overall server utilization increases.”

By the way, Arm is not advocating for some kind of golden agentic AI benchmark. Arm is instead advocating for a methodology that combines established component benchmarks with agentic workload measurements and end-to-end task evaluation. Benchmarks such as InferenceX and TPCx-AI can represent important portions of the workflow, including inference serving and the machine learning pipeline. But an agentic system also includes CPU-side orchestration, retrieval, state management, tool execution, sandboxing, security, and other activities that those discrete benchmarks were not designed to test.

“The goal is therefore to take a holistic view of the agentic flow while retaining component-level measurements that let engineers understand where performance differences originate,” says Defilippi. “Arm intends to characterize a broad set of these behaviors, from targeted component tests through higher-level metrics such as wall-clock task completion, agent density, and efficiency. The methodology is applicable to AGI CPU systems, but we are defining the workload and measurement framework rather than announcing a specific AGI CPU cluster benchmark.”

The methodology that Arm is proposing will not be restricted to CPUs, of course, because agentic AI doesn’t only run on CPUs. Component-level performance of not only CPUs, but also GPUs or other XPU accelerators, memory subsystems, and networking has to be measured, and we also have to pay close attention to how orchestration, retrieval, and tool deployment and execution all run. A useful agentic AI testing methodology needs both controlled component tests that expose individual bottlenecks and end-to-end tests that measure user outcomes.

When it comes to agentic AI, sequential latency – the bailiwick of the CPU, which is a moderately parallel compute engine that has cache hierarchies and clock speeds optimized to have high sequential processing capability – is a key constraint for task completion in an agent loop. The CPUs in the agentic AI infrastructure have to wait for GPUs or a mix of GPUs and XPUs to do the prefill token processing and the decode token output that drives the agentic workflow, spawning queries and activation of tools and often the generation of code.

“Single-threaded performance matters because many parts of an agent loop are latency-sensitive and sit on the critical path,” Defilippi says. “But it is only one dimension. Agent infrastructure also has to support many agents at once, so core count, memory bandwidth, cache capacity, scheduling efficiency and sustained performance under high utilization become increasingly important as concurrency rises.”

Obviously, benchmark measurement problems emerge when a single logical operation spans multiple dependent steps across the system.  An agent may reason about a task, invoke a tool, wait for a database or API response, update its state, return to model inference and then decide what to do next. Because later steps often depend on the results of earlier ones, latency accumulates across the critical path even when different parts of the underlying system can operate in parallel.

“Many agentic workflows therefore have both a latency problem and a concurrency problem,” explains Defilippi . “For an agent, the next action often cannot begin until the preceding dependency completes, so CPU-side execution, memory access, model inference, tool calls and network latency can all contribute to task-completion time. Reducing latency in the CPU-visible portions of that path can move the agent to its next action sooner and, where accelerators are involved, return work to the GPU or XPU sooner as well.”

“At the same time, the infrastructure is rarely running just one agent. Other agents and independent portions of a workflow can execute while one dependency is waiting. As concurrency increases, core count, memory bandwidth, cache capacity, scheduling efficiency and sustained performance under utilization become increasingly important. The system therefore has to balance responsive execution along each dependency chain with enough aggregate throughput to support many agents concurrently.”

That leads to a practical way to evaluate CPU performance at three levels. At the core level, measure latency and per-thread performance for work that sits on the critical path. At the system level, measure throughput, concurrency, memory behavior and sustained performance under high utilization. At the rack level, measure how much completed work the infrastructure can sustain within its power, cooling and physical constraints.

Component measurements explain why one platform behaves differently from another. End-to-end agentic measurements show whether those differences actually improve successful task completion.

In systems where accelerator inference is part of the agent loop, CPU performance can also affect how efficiently those accelerators are used. The CPU handles work such as request scheduling, orchestration, data preparation, runtime services and other functions around model execution. Delays on the CPU side can extend the overall task path, while efficient CPU execution can return work to the accelerator sooner. Infrastructure teams should therefore evaluate performance under realistic load and concurrency rather than relying only on lightly loaded peak results.

As has always been the case, the architecture of a system has to reflect the workload, and different choices for compute engines, memory, networking, and storage will be made based on the nature of those workloads. And, to make matters even more complex, it is very difficult to predict how the agentic AI workloads will evolve over the next few years. But there are considerations between latency and concurrency that will persist no matter how agentic AI architecture changes over the next four to five years – a span of time that matches how long machines installed in the field today will still be running.

Defilippi explains this interplay: “Where inference serving is part of the agent loop, CPU-visible functions such as scheduling, tokenization, serialization and KV-cache management can put pressure on the memory subsystem. That makes memory bandwidth, bandwidth per core, cache behavior and memory locality relevant to how efficiently the system advances.”

“Waiting for a tool response is different. The CPU can schedule other work while one agent waits on a database, API or sandboxed application. At low concurrency, that dependency has a large effect on an individual task's completion time. At higher concurrency, the ability to run other agents makes throughput, memory bandwidth and scheduling efficiency increasingly important.”

At scale, these measurements converge on the economics of the rack. Datacenters operate within fixed power, cooling, and physical constraints. The relevant question is no longer simply how much performance one processor can deliver, but how much useful agent work the infrastructure can sustain within those limits. Ultimately, what happens at the rack-level – and perhaps not too far into the future, what happens at the row-level – is what those implementing agentic AI will care about most.

“That is why metrics such as tasks per rack and energy per task become important alongside CPU-level performance,” says Defilippi . “More completed tasks within the same rack-level power envelope can translate directly into better infrastructure economics and lower task cost. Thermal headroom also gives the system capacity to absorb bursts of activity without compromising performance when demand rises. We would qualify the comparison with ‘scheduled batches,’ however, because some agentic workloads can themselves be batch-oriented. The broader point is that persistent, highly utilized agent services make sustained efficiency, density, and throughput per rack increasingly important, regardless of whether an individual task is interactive or batch.”

Arm has begun applying this framework to its AGI CPU. Using workloads aligned with the agentic methodology, Arm has sanctioned an independent, third party to evaluate AGI CPU performance against AMD EPYC Turin across CPU-visible parts of agentic workflows including tooling, orchestration and reasoning and planning.

The testing uses measured server-level performance as the basis for rack-level modeling and the results show approximately 2X the performance per rack compared with AMD EPYC 9755, demonstrating why performance at the rack level can tell a different story from an isolated core or socket benchmark.

When all is said and done, this may be the most complex capacity planning job that IT organizations have ever encountered. And they are going to need lots of help from component vendors and system makers to sort it all out because winging it and hoping for the best will be a very expensive proposition.

Sponsored by Arm

item.title: Intel’s $2.3 Billion Bet on a Quantum Future is a Decade in the Making
item.description:
READ MORE

  • Intel gets tax breaks while local authorities lose revenue, claims policy org

    4 hours ago

  • Humanity can't afford not to spend $800B on AI, Anthropic insists

    1 day ago

  • Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger bets on Nagare Labs to vault the memory wall

    2 days ago

  • AI’s epic cash call is matched only by its ability to strangle revenue streams

    9 days ago

  • New motherboards, old RAM, plenty of life left in yesterday's PCs

    14 days ago

Intel’s struggles for much of the past decade have been well documented here and in other news sites, industry analyst reports, and financial research papers. The once-dominant chip maker has been tripped up by any number of challenges, from the cutting into its server chip market share and Nvidia GPUs to billions in operating losses sustained by its . Intel in its FY 2026 second quarter, and the company is due to release is latest quarterly numbers on October 29.

Lip-Bu Tan, Intel CEO, is mid-turnaround, cutting costs and scaling back earlier expansion plans. The chipmaker is also benefiting from the , a more CPU-intensive workload that could narrow the gap between CPUs and GPUs in the fast-growing AI market.

Even so, innovation at Intel hasn't stalled. This week, the company signalled that quantum computing will be an important part its future, and executives are now ready to make a big bet on the rapidly evolving technology.

Intel announced plans to acquire six-year-old Israeli company $2.3 billion. The quantum software maker's platform helps developers build quantum algorithms and applications faster and at scale using tools like AI natural language models and a Python-like language. The deal is expected to close in the second half of next year.

As development of quantum computers accelerates, the focus of a growing numbers of companies like Classiq is expanding beyond hardware and qubits to software, algorithms, , , and .

Intel has spent the past decade quietly building out its quantum portfolio, which ranges from chips like its Tunnel Falls QPU, a 12-qubit silicon chip built with the spin-qubit modality, to its Quantum SDK and Horse Ridge control chips developed in 2019. The company also can manufacture its quantum chips using the same 18A-based process technology that it uses for its mainline CPUs.

Classiq should allow Intel to become a full-stack quantum company that can compete with the likes of and in a market tipped to grow to up to $20 billion in the next few years.

Classiq will turn what has been a lab project for Intel into a full commercial business, according to Intel chief technology officer Pushkar Ranade.

"This effort on quantum computing is really a preparing Intel for the future, for the next wave of computing,” Ranade told journalists during a call. “Up until now, our quantum computing group for the last 10 years was purely a research-and-development project. It wasn't really viewed as a commercial activity. But we feel that given all of the traction, all of developments in the marketplace, the timing is right to start making the next steps towards commercialization, which is another reason why the Classiq acquisition is so important for us. It moves our quantum computing group from just a research-and-development focus to an actual quantum computing business."

Nir Minerbi, Classiq co-founder and chief executive officer, said during the same call that the company – which Tan four years ago – saw an opportunity to fill a void in the quantum computing market, as hardware development and efforts to address challenges like error correction were evolving.

"There were quite a few players, several modalities, amazing progress, but there was not much of a software stack,” Minerbi said. “No OS, no compiler, no development environment. Basically, the development was limited to gate-level programming, which is a bit like designing a chip at the transistor level. We established Classiq to build the operating system for quantum, the environment that allows anyone to develop software for quantum computers, not only the quantum experts."

To make the software platform hardware-agnostic, Classiq had to embrace technologies that had been used to help scale classical computing, including EDA technologies, modeling, synthesis, and compilation. All of this important not only for Intel but also for the wider quantum computing field, he said.

"Any computing revolution so far was led by strong hardware, capable hardware, and software that unlocked its value,” Minerbi said. “In quantum, Intel has so many hardware assets: Its own QPU [quantum processing unit], silicon-based – which is the most promising modality — but also control electronics and foundry services and simulation stack and the quantum SDK and so on. When you accompany it with the software that engages with end users, it's a big move. Intel is in a great position not just to serve the end users, the enterprises, the governments, the universities and so on, but also to engage them with the rest of the quantum ecosystem, with quantum clouds and HPCs and datacenters and other hardware providers."

Classiq has more than four dozen enterprise customers, some of them major companies including communications giants Comcast and AT&T, car manufacturers BMW and Rolls-Royce, research centers like , and global IT firms like NTT Data and Mphasis. Once the deal closes, they’ll be customers of Intel, which Ranade admitted hadn’t "really done much by way of customer engagement or trying to commercialize our technology."

Minerbi claimed Classiq has generated "very healthy revenue this year" and looked forward to "very healthy revenue CAGR over the coming years." Classiq has raised some $200 million over multiple investment rounds over its six years, with valuation estimates ranging from $400 million to $600 million last year.

Classiq, which has about 130 employees, also brings much needed modality neutrality to Intel, which has pinned its hardware business on spin-qubits, where particles like electrons act like magnets that possess a property called "spin", which can give the particle a computational 0 or 1, or keep them in the quantum superposition of both. Scientists can control and entangle the spins using microwave pulses, magnetic fields, or electrical tuning to run quantum operations.

But there are a host of modalities in use, including superconducting by the likes of IBM, Google, and , neutral atoms by , Atom Computing, , and others, such as trapped ions ( and ), and photonics (PsiQuantum and Xanadu). It’s unclear which modalities – as the quantum computing field matures – will come to the forefront. A key feature of Classiq’s platform is that it can accommodate users of any modality.

This will be important for the large customers – which also includes Lufthansa and Wells Fargo – that may use quantum technology that isn’t spin-qubit, Minerbi said. "What we will give them from the Intel perspective is the assurance that no matter which modality it will be ... [Intel] will be ready."

Intel also will aggressively pitch its foundry capabilities for building quantum chips, Ranade said. He said the key reason for opting for spin-qubit as Intel’s modality was because "it lends itself very easily to manufacturing on conventional semiconductor equipment." Intel builds its QPUs and control electronic chips based on 18A logic technology at its fab in Oregon. There are versions of the technology specifically for the quantum chip – 18A-Q – and control chip (18A-C).

"We are open to being part of a quantum foundry for discrete components of this stack," Ranade said. "At the same time, we have already built multiple quantum computing systems, entire systems, and we also aspire to become a quantum system provider, as in to build the whole quantum computer."

Despite the enthusiasm of both companies for this deal, he cautioned that quantum is a long-term play.

"As a combined entity hardware-plus-software, we hope that there will be some synergies with [Classiq’s] quantum platform and our existing quantum hardware," he said. "We hope it will be a synergistic and attract even more customers. But this is not going to be a high-margin business from day one. This is really a bet on the future, and this is something we also have to do in addition to our mainstream businesses today." ®

item.title: Oracle is Expanding the Accelerator Options in OCI for Enterprises
item.description:
It’s a tale of two companies when discussion turns to Oracle and the burgeoning AI industry. The longtime tech giant tends at the same time to embody the surging enthusiasm about the technology’s promise and the looming concerns about the massive amounts being spent and the possibility of a bursting AI bubble.

On the latter, it’s a “yeah but” sort of story. The company’s sales between its 2025 and 2026 fiscal years jumped from $57.4 billion to $67.4 billion, and its Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) business in Q1 FY 2027 hit $7.4 billion, a 121 percent year-over-year jump . And there’s more to come. Its remaining performance obligations, which represent contracted sales for service not yet delivered and not counted in revenue, hit $664 billion, up $209 billion over the previous year.

But that comes amid spending worries, in particular the hundreds of billions of dollars it’s spent on building datacenters to support the exploding AI-driven demand. Its capital expenditures in FY 2026 hit $55.7 billion and could push beyond $90 billion this fiscal year, all against the backdrop of growing public resistance to datacenter buildouts and AI itself. Oracle certainly isn’t alone in this spending rush, but it’s often pointed to as a cautionary tale.

The Technology Itself

That said, move away from all the dollar signs and financial projections, and Oracle is aggressively expanding what it offers AI customers through its cloud business while holding its own in a market of other heavyweights, from Microsoft to Google to Amazon Web Services,

That’s what’s been on display at the Oracle AI World 2026 show in Las Vegas this week. The first day wasn’t an open floodgate of new products, services, and partnerships. Oracle executives put at the top of the agenda two relatively narrow but key aspects of enterprise AI: the security of the data and how the technology can ease the day-to-day for companies and their workers alike.

Day 2 had a greater focus on the architecture itself, adding key pieces to the OCI infrastructure to give organizations more hardware options as they take on greater inference and other AI workloads.

Both fit with Oracle’s push to ensure that enterprises and HPC customers can run their growing AI workloads using whatever software and hardware they need .

“There's more comfort with a wide range of options in those environments,” Nathan Thomas, senior vice president and product manager for OCI, told The Next Platform before the show. “We want to enable that, so we partner very deeply with who we view are best-in-breed in markets. You see us do a lot with Nvidia in chipsets. You see us do a lot with AMD chipsets. We feel very confident those are going to be solutions that our customers continue to want to see and we want to partner deeply there. We don't want to put ourselves in a position where we're dictating any of that stuff or trying to cut off any options for those customers.”

At the show on Tuesday, executives unveiled new accelerator choices. Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) will be available on OCI next year – the first time Google’s specialized AI chips will be offered in a hyperscale environment other than Google’s own. The chips are designed to handle large language model (LLM) training and post-training workloads and inference for reasoning and agentic AI.

Google, in April, released its eight-generation TPUs , the first model to split into two distinct specialized chips, the TPU 8t for training and TPU 8i (below) for inference.

Likewise, Oracle next year will deploy Cerebras’ fast-inferencing hardware into OCI. Cerebras, known for creating wafer-sized chips that put compute and memory on the same chip, in August introduced its CS-4 AI accelerator, a rack-scale offering based on three of its new Wafer Scale Engine 3 Turbo (below) chips, which the company boasts offers up to 30-times the tokens-per-second-per-user speed of GPUs. Those, too, will be arriving in OCI in 2027.

Another option will be SambaNova’s fifth-generation inference-focused SN50 Reconfigurable Dataflow Units (RDUs), (below) which were released in February. They’re designed to work with GPUs, with those accelerators handling prefill tasks and the RDUs handling decode.

Deep Trust

On Monday, Oracle unveiled its Deep Trust AI Architecture, which will be embedded in the company’s AI Database, Autonomous AI Database, and APEX AI Application Generator. The goal is to protect organizations’ data as AI applications are accessing sensitive information, AI agents are breaching systems of outside companies to complete their tasks, and threat groups are using AI in their attacks.

The architecture is designed to protect such data, enforce business rules, ensure accurate answers from AI systems, and control AI’s interactions with enterprise environments. Oracle wants to embed this control layer where the data lives. It dovetails with Oracle's Maximum Availability Architecture, which shows enterprises how to build systems that remain available even during failures.

“Deep Trust AI Architecture applies the same principle to AI: build trust into the architecture from the start, instead of trying to bolt it on later,” wrote Juan Loaiza, executive vice president of Oracle database technologies, and Maria Colgan, vice president of product management. “And, because that trust is enforced in the underlying infrastructure, rather than buried inside each application, it can protect both the applications you already have, and the new applications you build. ... AI should not have to implement enterprise trust every time it builds an application or accesses data. Trust should be built into the architecture.”

Oracle also is putting an emphasis on turning on more AI in the workplace. The company is expanding its partnership with OpenAI , linking the AI vendor’s models, ChatGPT chatbot, and Codex developer tool with its own applications, data, and cloud infrastructure. This opens another door for frontier AI to get deeper into the enterprise, touching on everything from building applications to detecting and fixing security vulnerabilities.

Oracle is offering ChatGPT plug-ins in Oracle AI Workspace to let enterprises connect to OpenAI tools with Oracle’s Fusion applications, NetSuite, AI Database, and OCI, making their capabilities ready for agents and accessible to ChatGPT users.

New AI-fueled features in Oracle’s Fusion portfolio are aimed at making agentic AI a key player in the enterprise by letting users define what they want and letting tools do the work.

“Work is sometimes organized around the work itself,” Co-CEO Mike Sicilia said during his opening day keynote. “People need to know what applications to open, where to find the information, the steps to follow, and who is to do what’s next. AI allows us to do that much better. It allows for far more intuitive software. In fact, AI should allow you to barely think about the software at all. Instead of navigating applications and managing processes, you simply tell the system what you’d like to accomplish. Because it understands your business, it can figure out how to get the work done.”

Oracle also rolled out new applications powered by its Fusion Claw, the execution runtime behind the Fusion Agentic Applications suite. At the show, the company unveiled 25 new agentic applications across Oracle Fusion software suites, from human resources and ERP to supply chain and customer management, for tasks like scheduling deliveries, customer service evaluations, and payroll management. Customers also can build their own agentic applications.

Fusion Companion gives users an avenue to work with Fusion Application through ChatGPT and other AI tools. It takes what users ask for and automatically selects and coordinates the agents, workflows, approvals, and other steps to execute the work. Oracle also announced Fusion Setup and Configuration Registry, a public Git repository to make implementing Fusion applications easier and faster. The vendor’s expertise and best practices become reusable AI skills agents can use to automate what are now manual setup and configuration tasks.

item.title: Nvidia Simulates Its Way Into Google's Magic State Cultivation Party
item.description:
There’s a lot of innovation happening in the quantum computing field as it moves closer to the promised land of practical, scalable fault-tolerant systems. That said, reducing errors in calculations remains a core challenge that needs to be solved. Qubits are extremely fragile, can easily fall apart and lose their coherence, and a quantum system that makes too many errors is not useful.

Quantum computing vendors create logical qubits from a collection of many physical qubits that can detect, isolate, and fix errors without interrupting the underlying quantum state. But it’s difficult to scale quantum systems when a single logical qubit could require thousands of physical qubits . And the scalability difficulties don't end there.

Universal quantum systems – those that can run all operations already performed by classical servers plus those specific to quantum computers – need to include both Clifford gates (like S and CNOT gates) and non-Clifford gates (like T gates) to perform quantum algorithms. Most error correction codes can handle Clifford states, but not non-Clifford gates.

In 2004, researchers introduced magic gates, which are prepared by the computer and injected into the computation. They are key to universal quantum computation, but they're also fragile, difficult to create with high fidelity, and can't be used again, so more have to be continuously created. Magic state distillation was used to offset this by collecting many noisy – or inaccurate – states and turning them into fewer, high-fidelity magic states. However, doing all of this takes time and can consume as much as 95 percent of a quantum system's capacity, creating a troubling resource bottleneck.

Google researchers in 2024 introduced another technique – magic state cultivation – to more cheaply and efficiently generate high-fidelity magic states. Rather than create huge numbers of noisy states and then discard a lot of them, with cultivation, engineers can put a noisy state into a small area on the quantum chip and then – like a filter – run measurements via special coding techniques to find errors and remove flawed tries, eventually growing a lower-error magic state and significantly driving down the hardware overhead needed to run quantum algorithms.

Putting Cultivation to Test

On October 15, both Google and Nvidia announced projects they say significantly advance the development of magic state cultivation, with Google Quantum AI researchers reporting the first hardware implementation of the method. Running it on Google’s Willow superconducting quantum chip , the demonstration resulted in a 40-fold reduction in errors compared to uncultivated states and created T-states that reached 99.99 percent in logical fidelity.

Less than a week later, Nvidia researchers announced that they’d run a 104-qubit simulation on Jupiter – Europe’s first exascale computer housed at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Germany and powered by Nvidia GH200 superchips – that tested magic state cultivation, which they said uses 90 percent fewer qubits than other methods.

Sam Stanwyck, director of quantum product at Nvidia, told reporters the work of both vendors was a critical step in eventually reaching fault-tolerant quantum computing, and that Nvidia shows the critical role that such simulations can play.

“This is complementary to Google's work,” Stanwyck said. “What Google did is a small-scale demonstration of this in hardware. It was a proof-of-concept that magic state cultivation, the approach, actually works on real hardware. The next steps for Google and for everyone are now, how do you design around that and how do you scale it up? What everyone will want to do to enable that is simulate magic state cultivation to understand it much better and design the next generation of processors. What our result does is point the way with tools and a platform for how to do that.”

After two years of working to move cultivation from theory to reality, Google scientists outlined the work and results in a paper published in Science . They noted they need to demonstrate the technique at a larger scale to make it more realistic for a practical quantum system, but added that “this achievement takes a key theoretical idea and turns it into an experimentally demonstrated reality.”

Nvidia’s Stanwyck said the company’s work illustrated how simulations can push this along, arguing that “in order to be able to effectively design hardware and software around these approaches, you need to simulate it as deeply as possible to understand how it behaves and, especially, how it handles errors.”

The vendor – which wants to be the accelerator for future hybrid quantum-classical environments – is not the only one using a digital twin to run simulations to address error correction. Earlier this year, scientists with Amazon Web Services and Quantum Elements – along with the University of Southern California and Harvard University – wrote about their work in the area.

Nvidia scientists used its CUDA-Q quantum-classical platform and cuQuantum software development kit to create detailed simulations of hardware errors – including coherent errors – and leakage.

“ These are the small, small systematic mistakes in quantum operations that accumulate over a computation and limit what the computer can do,” Stanwyck said. “They were able to simulate that in detail and simulate the effect on the algorithm. Now we're now able to test how magic state cultivation responds to these effects, which helps the researchers work out what the quantum hardware needs to do, how to build it, what code to run, and what to improve before building the next version.”

Nvidia researchers started the project on a GB200 NVL72-powered system at its Accelerated Quantum Research Center in Boston to develop and validate methods needed to prepare the software to run on a system the size of Jupiter, he said. The development platform was used to scale tests from four GPUs to hundreds, eventually moving it to 8,192 GPUs on Jupiter.

“With magic state cultivation, we were able to simulate from the physics to the application and actually let researchers and those who are developing quantum computers connect a deep understanding of errors in the physical qubits and how they affect application runtime so they can design better [magic] state cultivation, design better quantum computers, and ultimately, this is how simulation can help pull in the timeline to useful quantum computing,” he said.

item.title: Cadence, Nvidia Unveil New AI Models To Put EDA On Autopilot
item.description:
Like a virus, generative AI has invaded nearly every facet of technology, including chip and system design. If you ask Cadence Systems senior VP Paul Cunningham, somewhere between 20 and 30 percent of chips under development today are being designed with the help of AI agents, and that number is growing rapidly.

In many ways, Cadence's latest products are among the clearest examples of how generative AI and HPC will coexist not just in industry but the sciences as well.

Over the past year or so, the EDA giant has rolled out a series of so-called "AI Super Agents," including AuraStack for advanced packaging and PCB layout, ChipStack for SoC design and verification, InnoStack for PHY routing, and ViraStack for analog circuit design.

Much like Anthropic's Claude Code or OpenAI's Codex, these harnesses are designed to work with LLMs to automate design and testing flows by orchestrating Cadence's existing EDA, test, and verification tools. This works for much the same reason that AI code assistants have exploded in popularity among software engineers. Code either compiles or it doesn't. Similarly, Cadence has tests to verify and validate its designs will work as intended.

But just like many code assistants, the effectiveness of these tests depends heavily on how closely their training data resembles the inputs and outputs they're fed. Cadence's early agents were largely powered by off-the-shelf LLMs, which limited exposure to something like RTL.

“It’s not the case that these amazingly powerful out-of-the-box foundation models are just going to do everything. They’re the starting point, and you can still specialize,” Cunningham said.

In a bid for greater specialization, this week Cadence announced a partnership with Nvidia and launched its Maestro AI model family. These models were fine-tuned on Nvidia's Nemotron family of models to work with and interpret the results of Cadence's own tools.

Not surprisingly, better domain knowledge tends to translate into better results. If Cadence is to be believed, early testing of its Maestro models showed an "up to" 30 percent increase in output quality and "up to" 5x greater token efficiency versus general purpose foundation models. In other words, post-trained models on Cadence's tools made them both smarter and cheaper to run.

Along with the models, Cadence's Maestro platform also allows for customization based on customer data, although Cunningham tells us this will be offered more as managed service than something customers figure out on their own.

Much like its existing agent harness, Cadence's Maestro models and agents can access the models via API, run in a secure VPC, or assuming you've got the hardware necessary, on prem.

Cadence isn't the only one exploring the use of AI agents to orchestrate HPC workloads. Nvidia has been pushing HPC into a collision course with AI for years now, which makes sense when you consider its GPUs are good for more than training and running AI, even if that’s what most folks are buying them for.

This concept of AI-driven labs is also a core component of the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission , under which we've seen a flurry of new large Nvidia-based supercomputers.

As you may recall, researchers at Sandia National Labs recently demonstrated how AI agents could be used to develop and test new hypotheses in what they described as a self-driving lab, although those tests didn't have the benefit of modern agent harnesses or even LLMs.

Given the limited funding afforded public researchers, it's easy to see why the idea of an AI lab assistant capable of carrying out tasks long after you've gone home for dinner might be attractive.

item.title: APC says let there be light, with raft of standards to speed up photonics manufacturing
item.description:
The Advanced Photonics Coalition has given the green light for a slew of standards it says should allow “high volume manufacturing” of optical networking kit.

The announcement, at the PECC Summit earlier this week, comes amidst concerns about shortages of key components and materials needed for manufacturing optical networking gear, even as the surging AI industry starts hitting the “copper wall.” As Gbps demands rise, copper’s reach gets ever shorter, while heat emissions and energy consumption increases.

But the photonics industry is struggling to scale. Earlier this month, Lumentum Holdings told Bloomberg that its optical components are “completely sold out” through to 2029, and it won’t be able to meet demand for some products between now and 2028. The company produces indium phosphide components which are critical for photonics. China is a major producer of indium phosphide adding an extra level of geopolitical stress to the supply chain.

Lumentum’s backers include Nvidia, whose founder and CEO Jensen Huang demonstrated its Spectrum X co-packaged optics-based technology at GTC this week .

“So we now have extremely high data rate, extremely high quality data that comes directly onto the chip, and this goes directly into transceivers without going through a PCB and a transceiver goes right into the optics,” enthused Huang.

More broadly, datacenter operators are banking on optical to deliver more data to their pricey GPUs and increase efficiency as the technology requires less power and produces less heat.

Earlier this month, McKinsey flagged networking as one of the areas that “requires improvement” as AI becomes more and more about inference, advising operators “deploy optics-integrated switches (CPO) for higher bandwidth density and lower power per bit.” And it flagged up the need for “open interconnect” saying “a specialized architecture only earns it cost at volume.”

But statements like Lumentum’s raise the fear that optical networking components are heading towards the sort of shortages – and surging prices - already plaguing high end DRAM and flash storage.

The APC said this week that “By establishing common manufacturing, interface, and test practices, APC aims to remove implementation variations that add no market value and overcome supply chain silos that constrain volume.”

Its standards portfolio “supports multiple sourcing and broader supplier participation, helping the industry build an open and scalable photonics ecosystem.”

The portfolio covers:

• System Level Architecture Overview for Co-Packaged Optics

• Co-Packaged Optics Informative Outlook and Recommended Practices

• Silicon Photonics for Co-Packaged Optics Recommended Test Practices

• 4-Core Multicore Fiber Cable, Connector and Fiber Array Unit Specification

• Silicon Photonics Manufacturing Specification

Photonics developer Resolight is one of the companies on the APC working group.

“There are two technologies that today are independent and actually co-deployed in scale up,” said Ofer Shapiro, Resolight CEO. “One is traditional slow switching OCS that they're using to reconfigure the network. And the other one is data switches that are working 1,000 times faster.”

Resolight sees the APC standards as an endorsement of its Nanosecond optical circuit switching approach, addressing the protocol integration needed to enable native photon routing through nanosecond optical circuit switching (OCS).

“Native photon routing extends optical switching into the data plane itself, directing coordinated data transfers through the network while keeping their payloads in the light domain,” it said in a statement.

By reducing repeated optical to electrical to optical conversions, its architecture could deliver a massive boost in network energy efficiency and dramatically reduce the number of optical transceivers needed in multi-rack AI scaleup networks.

“The APC CPO specifications address the data-plane integration needed to make native photon routing a practical alternative to electronic data switching,” Shapiro added in Resolight’s statement.

“The easiest to source and the greenest transceiver is the one that you don't need,” Shapiro told us.

He added that if Indium Phosphide supplies were a concern, the sensible response was to “need less of it rather than figure out where do we get more.”

In its " Co-Packaged Optics Informative Outlook and Recommended Practices " document released this week, the APC said, “Without open ecosystem driven standards, the natural gravitational pull is toward vertically integrated proprietary solutions, an outcome that would fragment the market, increase customer lock-in risk, slow adoption, and ultimately diminish the opportunities of innovation for CPO’s technical benefits.”

When it comes to Nanosecond-Level OCS, it said: “The objective is not to standardize a particular fast OCS implementation, but to define the control-plane, optical-interface and behavioral framework that allows fast, transparent OCS to operate as a first-class component of an open AI scale-up fabric.

Earlier this year, Chris Sharp, the chief technology officer at data centre operator Digital Realty, told the BBC , "I think we're at the end of copper" with networking increasingly becoming the key factor slowing down compute.

item.title: PARTNER CONTENT: Three Physical Walls Are Hitting AI Datacenter Infrastructure at the Same Time - And the Compound Effects Are Worse
item.description:
Here is a trajectory that should focus the mind of anyone designing AI infrastructure right now. In 2023, a typical accelerator rack consumed around 20 kW and each chip dissipated roughly 350 watts. By 2024, rack power climbed to 50 kW; chip power hit 700 watts. In 2025, we crossed the kilowatt-per-chip threshold - racks reached 120 kW, individual processors exceeded 1,000 watts, and heat flux density landed between 50 and 100 W/cm². The current generation, shipping in 2026, pushes racks to 240 kW, chips past 2,000 watts, and heat flux to 120 W/cm².

The next generation - already in validation at multiple hyperscalers - targets megawatt-class racks, 3,000-plus watt chips, and heat flux densities above 200 W/cm².

That is not a gentle curve. It is a step function that breaks three things at the same time: cooling, power delivery, and electrical interconnect. At the 2026 OCP Global Summit in San Jose, xFusion's Director of Product Management Arthur Wang walked through the engineering detail behind all three in a keynote titled "Next-Generation Power & Cooling Solutions." What made the talk notable was not any single product announcement but the framing: these three constraints are not independent. They interact, they compound, and solving any two while ignoring the third still results in stranded infrastructure.

xFusion calls this "computing-power synergy." The less catchy, more precise description: co-optimizing the entire energy conversion chain from grid to transistor - cooling, power delivery, and interconnect treated as coupled variables rather than separate procurement categories.

The thermal wall: materials science versus Moore's Law

Air cooling is finished for high-density AI racks. That is no longer a controversial statement. The question is how much headroom the liquid cooling solutions being deployed today actually provide - and whether they will survive the next chip generation without a forklift upgrade.

The physics are straightforward. At 200-plus W/cm², convective air cooling cannot extract heat fast enough to prevent thermal throttling, regardless of plenum geometry or fan configuration. Direct liquid cooling - specifically cold plate-based DLC - is the only viable path. But a cold plate is only as good as the materials and micro-channel geometries inside it.

xFusion's approach is to use diamond-copper composite cold plates. The numbers: equivalent thermal conductivity exceeding 650 W/m·K, roughly twice that of pure copper (385–400 W/m·K). The cold plate design uses non-uniform fin geometries mapped to chip hot spots, yielding an average heat flux handling capacity of 200 W/cm² across the full cold plate area and over 400 W/cm² at localized hot spots. Total single-chip cooling capacity exceeds 4,000 watts.

That 4,000-watt figure matters because it provides roughly 33 percent headroom above the incoming 3,000-watt chip generation. In liquid cooling, headroom is not luxury - it is insurance against the silicon roadmap moving faster than the mechanical refresh cycle.

The material matrix behind this is broader than a single cold plate. xFusion presented five core thermal interface and heat-spreading materials at OCP, each targeting a different cost-performance point: graphene thermal pads (130 W/m·K, filling irregular gaps at 0.3–5 mm thickness), high-density copper skived cold plates (385–400 W/m·K, the workhorse for current-generation chip cooling), liquid metal TIM (30 W/m·K but with interface thermal resistance as low as 0.02 °C·cm²/W, eliminating microscopic air gaps), pure diamond cold plates (800–2,500 W/m·K, for extreme heat spreading), and the diamond-copper composites described above (550–800 W/m·K, combining diamond's conductivity with copper's machinability).

Looking further out, the company is developing two-phase jet cooling - using the latent heat of liquid-to-gas phase change rather than single-phase sensible heat to absorb energy from the chip surface. The advantage is dramatically reduced coolant flow rates for the same thermal load. The engineering challenges - sealing at scale, pressure management, blind-mate fluid connectors for serviceability - are substantial, but so is the thermal runway if single-phase DLC is the only option and chip heat flux keeps climbing.

For current deployments, xFusion's FusionPod for AI V8 - a 42U modular liquid-cooled rack rated at up to 155 kW - ships with a distributed CDU architecture requiring zero secondary piping modifications. That last detail matters more than it sounds. Retrofitting liquid cooling into an existing facility typically means ripping up floors to install secondary coolant loops - a process measured in quarters, not weeks. Eliminating that dependency compresses deployment timelines from years to months.

The electrical wall: why 48V-class distribution cannot survive the megawatt era

Cooling and power delivery are often treated as separate disciplines. They are not. Every watt delivered to a chip must leave as heat. The path that watt travels - from utility transformer through conversion stages to the voltage regulator on the board - bleeds energy at every step.

At today's standard 48V-class bus voltages (54V nominal), the current required for megawatt-scale racks is staggering. A 10 kW rack draws 185 amps. A 40 kW rack: 741 amps. A 120 kW rack: 2,222 amps. A 240 kW rack: 4,444 amps. A 500 kW rack: 9,259 amps. And a 1 MW rack: 18,519 amps.

The I²R loss implications are brutal. Copper busbar losses scale with the square of current. When rack power increases 25× (from 40 kW to 1 MW), current increases 25× - but resistive losses increase 625×. At 1 MW per rack with 54V distribution, busbar copper losses alone can exceed 50 kW. That is the power consumption of an entire server, wasted as heat in the busbar before a single floating-point operation is performed. And the busbars themselves become impractical objects - copper conductors weighing upwards of 200 kg per rack, creating structural and thermal challenges of their own.

The solution is straightforward in principle and formidable in execution: raise the distribution voltage. Moving from 54V to 800V DC - a factor of roughly 14.8× - reduces current by approximately 15× and I²R losses by approximately 220×. Simultaneously, the number of power conversion stages drops from four (in legacy AC/54V architectures) to three, pushing end-to-end system efficiency from roughly 88 percent to above 90 percent, and compressing line losses from 5 to 8 percent to below 1 percent.

xFusion is building toward this with its 800V HVDC Sidecar - a next-generation power supply prototype engineered for 300 kW to 1.2 MW configurations per rack. The roadmap also includes a direct 800V HVDC architecture that eliminates additional conversion stages entirely and natively supports green power integration - a detail that becomes increasingly important as grid-tied renewable capacity and behind-the-meter generation become standard features of new AI campuses.

Underpinning the voltage transition is a shift in semiconductor devices. xFusion is deploying wide-bandgap materials across the power conversion stack: SiC MOSFETs for AC-to-HVDC rectification (PFC + LLC topology, 100–300 kHz switching), GaN HEMTs for HVDC-to-DC conversion (LLC resonant, 800 kHz–1 MHz), and GaN-based multi-phase voltage regulators for the final 54V-to-12V/6V stage at 500 kHz to 1 MHz. Higher switching frequencies translate directly to smaller magnetics and higher power density - critical when every cubic centimeter of rack space is contested.

The company is also advancing vertical power delivery - placing power conversion modules directly behind the chip package rather than routing current laterally across the motherboard. This shortens the power path by roughly 90 percent, reducing both resistive losses and the transient response challenges that emerge when thousands of amps must be delivered to a processor that can swing its current draw by hundreds of amps in microseconds.

The interconnect wall: copper at 224G and beyond

The third constraint gets less attention but is equally binding at scale. Electrical signaling over copper traces at 224 Gbps per lane is already operating at the ragged edge of signal integrity. Channel loss, insertion loss, and crosstalk at these frequencies demand extraordinary equalization and error correction. Beyond 224G, the physics of copper become unforgiving.

The transition to optics is underway. Co-packaged optics (CPO) - placing photonic engines directly on or adjacent to switch silicon - collapses the distance penalty that limits electrical reach and unlocks bandwidth density that copper backplanes cannot match. For AI training clusters running thousands of accelerators in tightly coupled scale-up domains, interconnect bandwidth directly determines how large a distributed job can scale and how efficiently inference workloads distribute.

xFusion has commercially deployed 224G high-density orthogonal backplanes and is conducting pre-research on 448G. Its Super Node architecture - an open-architecture liquid-cooled system - delivers up to 240 kW per rack, supports 128 XPU per cabinet and 256 XPU across dual cabinets, and is designed for multi-vendor processor compatibility from the ground up. That openness is not philosophical - it is a hedge against the accelerator market's rapid fragmentation, where locking into a single vendor's proprietary interconnect fabric trades a bandwidth constraint for a supply chain dependency.

The compound problem

None of these three walls - cooling, electrical, optical - respects the others' timeline. They are all arriving in the same product generation. And they interact in ways that make partial solutions dangerous.

World-class liquid cooling paired with legacy 54V power delivery? The electrical bottleneck throttles the rack before the coolant warms up. Pristine 800V DC power feeding a cluster with inadequate optical fabric? Stranded GPUs waiting for data. High-bandwidth networking behind a thermally throttled compute tier? Wasted tokens. Wasted capital.

This is why the "computing-power synergy" framing - treating cooling, power, and interconnect as a single coupled optimization problem from grid to chip - is more than a marketing theme. It is an engineering discipline. And it is why xFusion has invested in the full vertical stack: from chip-level thermal interface materials and cold plates, through board-level and rack-level power conversion, to cabinet-scale liquid cooling and backplane interconnect.

The company's participation in more than 60 industry organizations, contribution to more than 60 open standards, and ecosystem of over 30,000 partners worldwide reflects a bet that no single vendor can solve the converged problem alone - but someone has to integrate the pieces coherently.

As Wang put it at OCP: "In the Agentic era, competitiveness is not about how many chips you have. It is about how much real business value you can extract from every watt and every joule of heat."

That statement maps to a value chain xFusion presented on stage -WATT → FLOPS → TOKEN → AGENT → VALUE - where each stage introduces conversion losses and the facility's true performance is measured not by watts consumed but by the useful business outcomes produced. It is, in essence, an argument that the AI datacenter is not a building that houses computers. It is an energy conversion system. And three physical walls are about to determine who converts efficiently and who does not.

item.title: How Mixx Technologies Is Lighting The Way To Fully Optical Scale-up Networks
item.description:
Modern rack systems like Nvidia's NV72 are packed with miles of copper flyover cables which form the substrate by which six dozen or more GPUs are made to work as one. Now, with Nvidia and others eyeing even larger scale-up fabrics, optics are unavoidable. But as the scale-up domain grows, so does the number of fibers spilling out the back.

That's the first problem photonics startup Mixx aims to solve. Founded in 2023 by Vivek Raghuraman and Rebecca Schaevitz, the company's first product, unveiled earlier this year, packs 64 fibers into a single connector called SxC.

"We can put 1,000 fibers within 800mm2," Raghuraman told .

Beyond the bigger fiber attach, Raghuraman argues that the rise of large scale-up compute domains necessitate a new way of thinking about how we build systems, one where the rack's backplane functions as an optical interposer for the silicon inside. Untethered from the limitations of copper, he sees a path toward a fully optical compute fabric.

To support this vision, Raghuraman says, Mixx is also developing a series of optics tech including near-packaged and copackaged optical engines, optical circuit switches, and a software control plane to manage it all. "It’s a three-pronged roadmap that we are developing to enable optical scale-up networks."

But this won't happen overnight — something that Raghuraman is not only aware of, but actually underpins the company's strategy.

No shortage of photonics vendors have come and gone with similarly ambitious claims, but it's worth noting this wouldn't be the first or even second time Raghuraman has built an optical engine. His team was responsible for several breakthroughs in silicon photonics during his seven-year career at Intel and was directly involved in the development of Broadcom's copackaged optical switches, which we've looked at on several occasions

“We are not just making solutions that are proof of concepts, but something that can be deployed by the hyperscalers,” Raghuraman said. And that means Mixx will be timing its product releases with market demand.

Let there be light

With its Vera Rubin Ultra rack systems, Nvidia is expanding its NVLink Switch fabrics from 72-144 to 576 and eventually 1,152 GPUs with the help of optics. Communications inside each rack will remain copper, but the communications between racks will be carried by light.

Nvidia hasn't said exactly how this is going to work yet. If we had to guess, Nvidia will integrate near-packaged or copackaged optics into its NVSwitches. Assuming one fiber pair per SerDes (serializer/deserializer), Vera Rubin NVL576 will need around 20,736 fiber pairs to connect the eight NVL72 racks it's assembled from. That's 2,592 fibers pairs per rack.

There are plenty of ways that Nvidia could get that number down, such as dense wave division multiplexing, which packs more wavelengths onto a single fiber. But even with 16 wavelengths per fiber, that's a lot of fiber to clean and terminate.

This is the exact reason why Raghuraman and his team are focusing on the connector first. Anyone building a scale-out network using optics, whether that be AMD, Nvidia, or one of Broadcom or Marvel's XPU partners, is going to need a denser fiber attach.

Mixx's next step will be an near-packaged optic (NPO) engine which could be integrated into a GPU node. While copackaged optics (CPO) integrated directly into ASIC packages are Mixx's ultimate goal, Raghuraman recognizes that the market simply isn't ready for that just yet.

NPO is generally seen as the safer option because if an optical engine fails, it won't render the GPU a paperweight; in theory it could be refurbished. Mixx aims to bring its first NPO module to market sometime in 2028 or 2029.

With NPO it becomes possible to do away with copper interconnects, flattening the scale-up topology from two tiers to one big one.

It’s going to take the “pragmatic adoption of the near package optics, because that’s what gets optics close to the switch or a compute... Once it’s all proven in the NPO form factor, then it transitions to a true co-packaged optics,” Raghuraman said.

Raghuraman expects Mixx's first CPO product to arrive some time around the end of the decade, right around the time when SerDeses are no longer viable for scale up networking.

Where we're going, we don't need SerDes

SerDeses are commonly used in high-speed networking when data needs to be sent over relatively long distances. But they have their limits. At 400 Gbps, the longest a signal can travel over copper without degrading is about 1.25 meters. Double the data rate, halve the reach. You can start to see where the problem lies.

But with CPO, the electrical signal needs only to reach the optical engine a few millimeters away, at which point reach becomes a non-issue for datacenter deployments. The move away from SerDes has other benefits with respect to scale up networks.

These networks typically feature 72 or more GPUs in an all-to-all fabric. Every GPU can talk to every other GPU with the help of a couple packet switches like Nvidia's NVSwitch or Broadcom's Tomahawk 6.

How large a single layer scale-up fabric can grow is limited in large part by the accelerators' radix – or put another way, the number of ports each accelerator has. Nvidia's Blackwell generation had 36 200 Gbps links with two links going to each of the NVL72's 18 NVSwitch ASICs.

By ditching SerDeses, Raghuraman expects to achieve far greater radix than is possible using copper interconnects. "This is most optimized when you are able to get to the same densities as the die-to-die interconnects," he said.

That larger radix opens up some interesting possibilities. For one with enough ports per chip you might not even need packet switches at all. "If we can avoid packet switching, it improves latency,” he said, adding that for larger cluster packet switches will still play a role. "We are trying to move it to a higher layer of the network."

A fully optical scale-up fabric

As we've previously seen with systems like Google's TPU or Amazon's Trainium2 pods, it's entirely possible to build compute fabrics without packet switches.

The problem has been that limited chip-to-chip radix necessitated the use of 2D and 3D toruses, which are great for training and even inference on dense models, but aren't well-suited to mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures because these topologies require more hops than an all-to-all switched fabric. This is actually why AWS moved to a switched fabric similar to Nvidia's NVL72 setup for Trainium3.

But with a high-enough radix, that same all-to-all connectivity can be achieved by connecting the chips directly to one another. One-hop connectivity to any GPU in the cluster, no packet switches required. But while Mixx is trying to avoid using packet switches where possible, its ideal scale-up network won't exactly be switchless.

Alongside its CPO engines, it's also developing a high-density optical circuit switch (OCS). These appliances are famously used in Google's TPU clusters to resize pods and route around failed accelerators, just like a telephone switch operator would disconnect one call and connect another.

The major issue for Mixx is the current crop of OCS appliances lack the density required.

“The biggest challenge with OCS today is getting high-radix OCS switches. Most of the technologies today are 16x16, 32x32,” Raghuraman said.

That's underselling the technology a little. Coherent and others now have OCS appliances with hundreds of ports , but they're also enormous. Mixx will likely need OCS appliances with thousands of high-density ports, which would be untenable without an ultra-dense fiber attach like SxC.

It's also going to need a software control plane to manage those connections. Any time an OCS appliance is reconfigured, connections do drop. In all-to-all fabric, such blips aren't  that disruptive because there's always more than one path between two accelerators. But those changes still need to be scheduled appropriately, which has its own set of challenges.

While it'll be years before Mixx can fully realize its vision, at least the company's roadmap won't have it pushing out proofs-of-concept decades before market demand materializes, something that has plagued many photonics startups in the past.

item.title: Huang shrugs off protestors to kick off GTC Berlin with DSX Pods, Robots
item.description:
Jensen Huang kicked off GTC Europe by promising to cut the time to token at new datacenters from months to weeks, with a Vera Rubin-powered AI factory in a box.

The DSX Pod – essentially a containerized version of its DSX reference architecture – was the hardware highlight of the Nvidia CEO and founder’s keynote speech, which was much about assuring Europe that it had a future in the AI era and namechecking the vendor’s key partners such as Schneider Electric and Siemens Electric, as unveiling brand new tech.

Huang described the Pod as “bringing this full-stack platform into a factory-built integrated system.” According to a video it “starts with Vera Rubin NVL72. Seven liquid-cooled compute racks connected with 17 kilometers of Spectrum X cables form a Vera Rubin DSX pod. Vera Rubin DSX pods are integrated, fully cabled, and factory tested, then delivered in transportable containers.”

The design relies on dry cooling rather than traditional evaporative cooling, and 800V DC for “efficient power delivery.”

None of that is new in itself – they’re part of the standard DSX architecture. But NVIDIA is targeting the deployment and supply chain challenges facing datacenter operators.

“The scale at which we are now producing computing is unheard of ever. Unimaginable,” said Huang. “Well, even then, when you bring these systems onto your sites, there are still months and months of assembly, and you just heard 17,000 kilometers of wiring to connect just Spectrum X for the scale-out computing. It’s a crazy number.”

That’s why buildouts such as TeraWulf’s Lake Mariner site outside Buffalo New York run into shortages of electricians before they have to deal with shortages of GPUs and DRAM. Nearly half of the 1,800 trades on site are electricians.

But, said Huang, “Now suppose we were to do that all inside the supply chain, run everything up, build everything up, make sure that it runs completely, get it qualified, burnt in, and by the time we ship it, it is fully functional. The amount of cabling and on-site assembly is going to be greatly reduced.”

But, just as importantly, he said, “By moving this into the supply chain the amount of idle computing, the amount of idle computing that's going to be sitting inside at your datacenters will reduce dramatically.”

Afterall, he said, a 1GW datacenter costs about $50 billion, with operators expecting to generate revenues of $40bn off the back of that infrastructure.
